definitions.definition: A person abets an offence under the NDPS Act who instigates, aids, or facilitates its commission, or is a party to a criminal conspiracy to commit such offence, whether or not the offence is actually committed in consequence; this includes, within India, abetting or conspiring to commit acts outside India that constitute offences relating to narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances under the laws of that place or would constitute an offence if committed within India.
definitions.plain_english: Abetment means helping, encouraging, or assisting someone to commit a drug-related crime under the NDPS Act, even if the crime never actually takes place. A person can be guilty of abetment just by being involved in planning or supporting the offence. The law treats the abettor as equally punishable as the person who actually commits the crime.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based logistics agent knowingly arranges the transportation of heroin from Afghanistan into India for a drug syndicate, without physically handling the drug himself — he is liable for abetment of illegal import.

A pharmacist in Delhi repeatedly provides prescription pads and doctor signatures to a drug trafficker to obtain psychotropic substances illegally — the pharmacist commits abetment even if he never possesses the substances personally.

A financier in Chennai wires money to a network knowing it will be used to purchase commercial quantities of cocaine for distribution — this constitutes abetment and may also attract enhanced punishment under Section 31A.

A college student in Pune introduces a drug dealer to potential buyers and facilitates transactions via encrypted messages, without personally selling — this active facilitation constitutes abetment of the sale offence under the NDPS Act.

An Indian national residing in Dubai coordinates with smugglers in India over phone to arrange storage and onward movement of ganja — abetment applies even though the person is outside India, as the act would constitute an offence if committed within India.
what_it_covers: A person who instigates or encourages another to manufacture, possess, or traffic narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances under the NDPS Act.
Participation in a criminal conspiracy to commit any NDPS offence, whether or not the offence is ultimately carried out.

Acts of abetment committed within India targeting drug-related activities to be executed in a foreign country, provided those acts would constitute NDPS offences if done in India or are offences under the law of that country.
A person convicted previously of abetment of an NDPS offence who is subsequently convicted again, attracting enhanced punishment of one and one-half times the maximum sentence under Section 31.
Abetment of offences involving commercial quantities of narcotic drugs where prior conviction exists, potentially attracting the death penalty under Section 31A.
what_it_excludes: Mere knowledge or passive awareness of another person's drug-related activity, without active instigation, facilitation, or agreement to participate.
Acts of a person who unknowingly provides services (e.g., a courier who is unaware of the nature of the package) without culpable mental state or intention.
Independent commission of a substantive NDPS offence such as possession or sale, which is charged directly and not as abetment.
Acts committed entirely outside India that have no connection to India and do not involve Indian nationals or Indian territory at any stage.
Reporting or informing law enforcement about a suspected drug offence, which cannot constitute abetment even if the reported person is acquitted.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person's conduct qualifies as abetment under the NDPS Act determines whether they face the same punishment as the principal offender — including mandatory minimum sentences — even if the underlying offence was never completed; additionally, a prior conviction for abetment triggers the enhanced sentencing regime under Section 31 (one and one-half times the maximum) and, in cases involving specified drugs at commercial quantities, may attract the death penalty under Section 31A.

definitions.definition: Acquittal, as used in Section 68Z of the NDPS Act, refers to a formal judicial verdict by a competent court finding a person not guilty of charges under this Act or any corresponding law of any other country, which has either not been appealed against or, where appealed, has been finally disposed of in a manner that prevents the forfeiture of the concerned property.
definitions.plain_english: An acquittal means a court has officially found a person not guilty of the drug-related charges brought against them. Under the NDPS Act, once a person is acquitted and that acquittal becomes final (either no appeal was filed or the appeal process ended without enabling forfeiture), any property that was seized or frozen in connection with their case must be released back to them.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai trader is charged under the NDPS Act for allegedly financing a narcotics operation; his bank accounts and property are frozen. After a full trial, the Special Court in Mumbai acquits him due to insufficient evidence, no appeal is filed by the prosecution within the prescribed period, and his frozen assets are subsequently released under Section 68Z.

A Delhi businessman's properties are seized under Chapter VA of the NDPS Act on suspicion they were illegally acquired through drug trafficking. He is acquitted by the trial court; the prosecution appeals but the High Court upholds the acquittal and the forfeiture cannot be ordered, triggering the mandatory release of the seized properties.

A person arrested in Chennai in connection with an international narcotics smuggling network is tried and acquitted by the competent authority in India. The corresponding foreign conviction also does not sustain. With the acquittal finalized and the warrant of arrest withdrawn, all properties frozen under the NDPS Chapter VA proceedings are released.

An associate of a detenu whose property was frozen as illegally acquired property under NDPS is separately prosecuted and acquitted by the Special Court in Kolkata. Since the acquittal is not challenged by the State, the property linked to that associate is released in accordance with Section 68Z.

A relative of a drug offender whose assets were attached under Chapter VA provisions is acquitted of charges under a corresponding law of a foreign country. Upon submission of the foreign court's acquittal order before the competent authority in India, and confirmation that no further appeal is pending, the frozen properties in India are ordered to be released.
what_it_covers: A formal not-guilty verdict pronounced by a Special Court or competent court in India against charges under the NDPS Act, where no appeal has been preferred by the prosecution.
An acquittal that has been appealed by the prosecution but the appellate proceedings concluded in a manner that did not result in forfeiture of the accused's property.

An acquittal by a competent court in a foreign country under a corresponding law that mirrors NDPS offences, which is recognised for the purpose of releasing frozen or seized properties in India under Chapter VA.

A situation where a person referred to under Section 68A(2)(a), (b), or (cc) — including associates and relatives of the main accused — is individually acquitted of charges, entitling them to release of their specifically linked properties.
what_it_excludes: A discharge order at the stage of cognizance or framing of charges, which is separately treated under Section 68Z and does not constitute an acquittal on merits.
Cases where the acquittal has been appealed and the appellate court has set it aside or remanded the matter, as the finality required for property release has not yet been achieved.

Situations where a detention order has merely been set aside or withdrawn without an underlying acquittal, which are governed separately by the first sub-section of Section 68Z and do not constitute acquittal.
Compounding of offences or out-of-court settlements that do not result in a formal judicial verdict of acquittal by a competent court.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person has been acquitted under Section 68Z directly determines whether seized or frozen properties must be mandatorily released by the competent authority under Chapter VA of the NDPS Act. Without a qualifying acquittal (or discharge), the State retains the right to continue forfeiture proceedings, and the accused or associated persons have no automatic entitlement to recover their frozen assets.

definitions.definition: "addict" means a person who has dependence on any narcotic drug or psychotropic substance.
definitions.plain_english: An addict is someone who is physically or psychologically dependent on a narcotic drug or psychotropic substance, meaning they cannot easily stop using it without experiencing significant withdrawal or compulsion. This includes people hooked on drugs like heroin, cocaine, cannabis, or certain prescription medications that fall under the NDPS Act. The law treats such persons differently from traffickers, recognising their condition as one requiring treatment rather than purely punitive action.
real_world_examples: A young man in Mumbai who has been injecting heroin daily for two years and experiences severe withdrawal symptoms if he stops — he qualifies as an addict under the NDPS Act and may be referred to a de-addiction centre instead of being prosecuted.

A woman in Delhi found in possession of a small quantity of alprazolam (a psychotropic substance) for personal consumption, having developed a documented dependence on it after self-medicating — she may claim the benefit of Section 64A immunity by volunteering for treatment.

A daily labourer in Punjab caught consuming smack (diacetylmorphine) and showing clinical signs of opioid dependence — law enforcement may forward him to a registered treatment facility under Section 71 rather than prosecuting him.

A college student in Bengaluru repeatedly caught with small quantities of cannabis, whose doctor certifies he has cannabis use disorder — this certification of dependence positions him legally as an addict, potentially shielding him from imprisonment if he voluntarily seeks treatment under Section 64A.

A person in Chennai who was previously convicted for consumption of a psychotropic substance and who, upon re-arrest, presents medical evidence of continued dependence — courts may consider his addict status as a mitigating factor and direct him to a rehabilitation programme under Section 39.
what_it_covers: A person with clinically established physical dependence on heroin or other opioid narcotic drugs who cannot abstain without medical intervention.
An individual with documented psychological dependence on a psychotropic substance such as benzodiazepines or methamphetamine, even if no physical withdrawal is present.
A person found in possession of a small quantity of a narcotic drug solely for personal consumption arising from their established pattern of dependence.
Someone who voluntarily discloses their dependence to a drug treatment authority and seeks de-addiction treatment, thereby invoking protection under Section 64A.
A repeat offender for drug consumption whose medical records and expert testimony establish long-term substance dependence recognised under ICD or DSM diagnostic criteria.
what_it_excludes: A drug trafficker or dealer who may personally use narcotics but is primarily engaged in commercial distribution — their trafficking activity places them outside the protective ambit of the addict definition.
A person who has experimentally or recreationally used a narcotic drug or psychotropic substance on a few isolated occasions without developing any clinical dependence.
A licensed medical professional or pharmacist who handles narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances in an authorised capacity, even if they are incidentally exposed to such substances.
A person who manufactures, finances, or harbours illicit drug operations — the addict definition does not extend any protection to such persons regardless of whether they also personally use drugs.
An individual who falsely claims dependence without any medical evidence or clinical assessment to avoid prosecution — mere assertion of addict status without substantiation is insufficient.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as an 'addict' is legally decisive because it determines eligibility for immunity from prosecution under Section 64A when the person voluntarily seeks treatment, and it directs courts and authorities under Sections 39 and 71 to consider rehabilitation over punishment. Failure to recognise addict status can result in a person being wrongly prosecuted for possession or consumption offences that the Act intends to address through treatment rather than incarceration.

definitions.definition: Though not formally defined in Section 68B, 'adequate consideration' refers to a fair and reasonable price or value paid by a transferee for a property, commensurate with the market value of that property at the time of transfer, such that the transfer cannot be characterised as a sham or gratuitous transaction. A transferee is protected from forfeiture under Chapter VA only if the property was acquired for adequate consideration in good faith, without knowledge of its tainted origin.
definitions.plain_english: Adequate consideration means paying a fair and proper price for a property — roughly what it would fetch in the open market — at the time it was bought. If someone buys a property connected to a drug offence but pays a genuine, reasonable price without knowing about the crime, they are protected from having that property seized by the government. It is the opposite of a token payment, gift, or below-market deal used to disguise transfer of ill-gotten assets.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai flat worth ₹1.2 crore is sold by a convicted drug trafficker to an unrelated buyer who pays ₹1.18 crore through a registered sale deed and bank transfer — this payment constitutes adequate consideration, shielding the buyer from forfeiture proceedings under Chapter VA.

A Ludhiana businessman purchases a commercial warehouse from a person later found to be involved in illicit drug trade, paying the full circle-rate-based stamp duty value of ₹85 lakh via RTGS — the payment is treated as adequate consideration, and the competent authority cannot forfeit the warehouse from the businessman.

A relative of a convicted NDPS offender transfers an agricultural plot to a third party for a documented sum of ₹40 lakh, which matches the prevailing market rate in that district as certified by a government valuer; the third-party purchaser successfully resists forfeiture by demonstrating adequate consideration was paid.

A Delhi jeweller unknowingly buys a residential property from an associate of a narcotics trafficker at full market value supported by independent valuation reports, bank loan documentation, and registered sale deed — the competent authority under Section 68D accepts that adequate consideration was paid and drops forfeiture proceedings against the jeweller.

A private company purchases equipment from a psychotropic substance offender at the prevailing tender rate after a competitive bidding process; since the consideration matches fair market value and the transaction is arm's-length, the equipment is not treated as illegally acquired property in the company's hands.
what_it_covers: A payment made by a third-party purchaser that matches the prevailing market or circle-rate value of the property at the time of transfer, supported by registered documents and verifiable banking records.

Transfer of property by a relative or associate of an NDPS convict to an independent buyer who pays a commercially reasonable price, thereby breaking the chain of tainted ownership under Section 68A(2)(d).

A sale supported by independent professional valuation, stamp duty paid on actual consideration, and fund transfer through formal banking channels, demonstrating that the price was commensurate with the property's worth.
Competitive tender or auction-based purchases where the price is determined transparently and corresponds to fair value, even if the seller turns out to be a person covered under Section 68A(2).
what_it_excludes: Token or nominal payments far below market value, such as transferring a property worth ₹1 crore for ₹1 lakh, which indicate a disguised gift or sham transaction rather than a genuine sale.

Transfers made without any monetary consideration, including gifts, inheritances structured to evade forfeiture, or property passed under a will from an NDPS offender to a relative, as no consideration is paid at all.

Payments made through cash or unaccounted means where the source of funds itself is traceable to illicit drug proceeds, since such a transaction cannot be regarded as a good faith payment of adequate consideration.
Below-market deals between the NDPS offender and a related or colluding party designed to create a paper trail of transfer while the offender retains beneficial ownership or control of the property.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether adequate consideration was paid is the decisive test under Section 68A(2)(d) and Section 68B's definition of 'illegally acquired property' to determine if a current or intermediate holder of tainted property is shielded from forfeiture proceedings initiated by the competent authority under Chapter VA; without proof of adequate consideration, the property remains 'illegally acquired property' liable to be frozen, seized, and forfeited to the Central Government under Sections 68F and 68G.

definitions.definition: An Administrator is an officer of the Central Government, not below the rank of Joint Secretary, appointed by order published in the Official Gazette under Section 68G to receive, manage, and dispose of properties seized or forfeited under Chapter VA of the NDPS Act, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed.
definitions.plain_english: An Administrator is a senior Central Government official (at least a Joint Secretary rank) appointed to take charge of properties that have been seized or forfeited under the drug law. Their job is to look after these properties, manage them properly, and when directed, sell or dispose of them on behalf of the Central Government. They can also call upon police and other government officers to help them take possession of such properties if someone refuses to hand them over.
real_world_examples: A Joint Secretary-level officer from the Ministry of Finance is appointed via a Gazette notification as Administrator to manage a luxury Mumbai apartment seized from a drug trafficker whose assets were attached under Section 68F of the NDPS Act.

After a Delhi court orders forfeiture of farmland in Punjab found to be proceeds of an opium smuggling network, the designated Administrator takes possession of the land, manages its agricultural income, and eventually disposes of it per Central Government directions.

A drug lord in Rajasthan refuses to surrender his seized fleet of trucks to authorities; the Administrator, invoking Section 68U, requisitions local police assistance to forcibly take possession of the vehicles.

An Administrator appointed under Section 68G coordinates with officers of the Narcotics Control Bureau and the Income Tax Department under Section 68T to manage and audit financial accounts and properties belonging to a narcotics syndicate that were frozen pending final forfeiture orders.

Following forfeiture of a commercial warehouse in Chennai used for storing psychotropic substances, the Administrator arranges for the property to be auctioned, with proceeds remitted to the Central Government's Consolidated Fund of India.
what_it_covers: A Central Government officer of Joint Secretary rank or above formally appointed via an Official Gazette notification to manage seized or forfeited drug-linked properties.
The function of receiving, managing, and maintaining properties in relation to which orders under Section 68F or Section 68-I have been passed, subject to prescribed conditions.
The authority to take physical possession of forfeited properties under Section 68U, including use of force and requisitioning police assistance when persons refuse to surrender such properties.
The power to dispose of properties forfeited to the Central Government as directed by the Central Government under Section 68G(3).
what_it_excludes: Officers below the rank of Joint Secretary to the Government of India, who cannot be appointed as Administrator regardless of their seniority within their own department.
State Government officers, as the Administrator must be an officer of the Central Government appointed specifically under Section 68G.

The competent authority or Appellate Tribunal, which are distinct statutory bodies under Chapter VA performing adjudicatory functions separate from the administrative and custodial role of the Administrator.
Private receivers, liquidators, or court-appointed administrators under civil or company law, who have no standing under Chapter VA of the NDPS Act.
Officers of the Narcotics Control Bureau or other agencies listed in Section 68T, who are designated only to assist the Administrator and do not themselves perform the functions of the Administrator.
definitions.why_it_matters: The appointment of an Administrator is the legal mechanism that gives the Central Government operational control over seized and forfeited drug-related properties, ensuring they are not dissipated, misused, or lost before or after final forfeiture orders. Without a validly appointed Administrator, the custody, management, and disposal of such properties under Chapter VA of the NDPS Act would have no legal authority, potentially exposing the entire forfeiture process to challenge and undermining the Act's objective of stripping drug offenders of their illicit proceeds.

Legal text: An Administrator is an officer of the Central Government, not below the rank of Joint Secretary, appointed by order published in the Official Gazette under Section 68G to receive, manage, and dispose of properties seized or forfeited under Chapter VA of the NDPS Act, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed.

definitions.definition: The term 'animal' is not formally defined in the NDPS Act, 1985, but is used consistently to refer to any living beast or creature capable of being used as a means of transport or conveyance for narcotic drugs, psychotropic substances, or controlled substances, including but not limited to horses, mules, camels, donkeys, bullocks, and elephants. It functions as a mode of transit subject to search, seizure, and confiscation under the Act.
definitions.plain_english: An 'animal' under the NDPS Act refers to any domesticated or working animal that can be used to carry or transport illegal drugs from one place to another. Just like a vehicle, an animal used to smuggle drugs can be stopped, searched, and seized by authorised officers. This is especially relevant in rural and border areas of India where animals are traditional means of transport.
real_world_examples: In Rajasthan near the Pakistan border, a camel is found carrying concealed packets of heroin sewn into its saddlebags; the NCB officer stops and searches the camel under Section 49 and seizes both the drugs and the animal.

In a hilly region of Himachal Pradesh, a mule is being used to transport charas across mountain passes where vehicles cannot travel; narcotics officers intercept and rummage through the goods loaded on the mule.

In Uttar Pradesh, a bullock cart is stopped on suspicion of transporting opium; while the cart is a conveyance, the bullocks pulling it qualify as 'animals' subject to stoppage and search under Section 49.

Along the Myanmar border in Manipur, a horse loaded with goods containing concealed psychotropic substances is intercepted by Assam Rifles; the animal along with the contraband is seized and liable to confiscation under the Act.

In a rural district of Madhya Pradesh, a donkey is used to transport illicitly cultivated poppy straw; the excise officer arrests the handler and confiscates the animal as it is found liable to confiscation under Section 42.

In Punjab near the Indo-Pakistan border, elephants used in a farm are found to have opium derivatives hidden in their howdah; customs officers exercise their power under Section 43 to seize the drugs and the animals involved.
what_it_covers: Camels, horses, mules, donkeys, bullocks, and elephants used to carry or transport narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances.
Any animal found in transit with goods that conceal or contain controlled substances, making it liable to seizure and confiscation.
Animals used by owners or occupiers to knowingly facilitate the commission of an offence under Section 25 of the NDPS Act.
Animals intercepted at public places or in transit under Section 43, along with the drugs and other articles found on them.
Any animal that officers have reason to believe is about to be used for transporting narcotic drugs, allowing pre-emptive stoppage under Section 49.
what_it_excludes: Mechanised vehicles, aircraft, ships, or motor conveyances, which are separately covered under the term 'conveyance' in the Act.
Wild or stray animals not under the control or use of any person and not employed as a means of transport for drugs.
Animals kept on premises purely for agricultural, domestic, or commercial breeding purposes with no nexus to drug transport or commission of an offence.
Animals seized in unrelated criminal or revenue proceedings not involving narcotic drugs, psychotropic substances, or controlled substances.
Inanimate objects or containers used to store drugs, even if shaped like or associated with animals.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether something qualifies as an 'animal' under the NDPS Act determines whether authorised officers can legally stop, search, seize, and confiscate it under Sections 42, 43, and 49, and whether its owner can be prosecuted for permitting its use under Section 25. Incorrect classification may render a search or seizure unlawful and could result in evidence being inadmissible or the accused being acquitted.

definitions.definition: "Appellate Tribunal" means the Appellate Tribunal referred to in section 68N, being the Appellate Tribunal constituted under sub-section (1) of section 12 of the Smugglers and Foreign Exchange Manipulators (Forfeiture of Property) Act, 1976 (13 of 1976), which hears appeals against orders made under section 68F, section 68-I, sub-section (1) of section 68K or section 68L of the NDPS Act.
definitions.plain_english: The Appellate Tribunal is a special court-like body that hears appeals from people who are unhappy with certain government orders related to freezing or forfeiture of property under the NDPS Act. It is not a newly created body but is the same tribunal that was already set up under an older law dealing with smugglers and foreign exchange violators. If a competent authority orders your property to be frozen or forfeited, you can challenge that order before this Tribunal.
real_world_examples: A drug trafficker in Mumbai has his residential property worth ₹2 crore ordered to be forfeited by the competent authority under section 68-I of the NDPS Act; he files an appeal before the Appellate Tribunal within 45 days challenging the forfeiture order.

A Delhi businessman whose bank accounts are frozen under section 68F of the NDPS Act as proceeds of illicit drug trade approaches the Appellate Tribunal, claiming the freezing order was issued without proper evidence linking him to narcotics trafficking.

An officer referred to in sub-section (1) of section 68E, aggrieved by the competent authority's order under section 68L releasing certain seized property belonging to a suspected drug lord in Chennai, prefers an appeal to the Appellate Tribunal seeking restoration of the forfeiture.

A Kolkata-based logistics company whose fleet of trucks is ordered to be forfeited under section 68K(1) after being found used for transporting heroin challenges the order before the Appellate Tribunal, arguing the vehicles were used without the company's knowledge.

A Pune resident whose inherited property is declared illegally acquired under the NDPS Act files an appeal before the Appellate Tribunal contending that the property was acquired through legitimate means and not traceable to any drug-related income.
what_it_covers: Appeals against orders of freezing of property made by the competent authority under section 68F of the NDPS Act.
Appeals against orders of forfeiture of illegally acquired property under section 68-I or sub-section (1) of section 68K of the NDPS Act.
Appeals filed by any officer referred to in sub-section (1) of section 68E who is aggrieved by an order of the competent authority under the relevant sections.
Appeals against orders made under section 68L concerning release or disposal of seized or frozen property.
Delayed appeals filed after 45 days but within 60 days, where the Appellate Tribunal is satisfied sufficient cause existed for the delay.
what_it_excludes: Criminal appeals against conviction or acquittal in NDPS drug offence prosecutions, which lie before the High Court or Sessions Court, not this Tribunal.
Appeals against orders of the Central Government or State Government relating to licensing, permits, or authorisations under Chapters II and III of the NDPS Act.
Appeals filed after the outer limit of sixty days from the date of service of the competent authority's order, which the Tribunal has no power to entertain.
Disputes relating to confiscation of goods or conveyances under section 63 of the NDPS Act, which are handled through a different adjudicatory mechanism.
Any body constituted specifically and exclusively under the NDPS Act itself — the Appellate Tribunal is borrowed from the SAFEMA, 1976 framework and does not originate from the NDPS Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a forum qualifies as the 'Appellate Tribunal' under section 68B determines whether an appeal against a freezing or forfeiture order by the competent authority is validly constituted and whether the Tribunal has jurisdiction to grant relief, stay, or modify such orders; filing an appeal before any other forum would be jurisdictionally incompetent and could result in the forfeiture order attaining finality.

definitions.definition: The expression 'arrears of land revenue' is not formally defined in the NDPS Act, but is used in Section 72 as a mode of recovery: any licence fee, other sum payable to the Central or State Government under the Act, or the whole sum named in a bond upon its breach, which remains unpaid after exhausting deduction and attachment-and-sale remedies, may be recovered from the person liable or from his surety as if it were an arrears of land revenue, invoking the coercive recovery machinery available under the applicable State land revenue laws.
definitions.plain_english: When someone owes money to the government under the NDPS Act — such as a licence fee or a penalty from a broken bond — and that money cannot be collected by simpler means like deducting it from money owed to them or selling their goods, the government can use the same powerful debt-collection tools that are used to collect unpaid land taxes. This typically means the government can seize and auction the person's property without going to court first, just as a revenue officer would do for unpaid agricultural tax arrears.
real_world_examples: A pharmaceutical company licensed to manufacture morphine fails to pay the annual licence fee to the State Government under the NDPS Act; after attempts to deduct the amount from pending dues fail, the State Revenue Department initiates recovery proceedings against the company's assets as if the unpaid fee were land revenue arrears under the relevant State Land Revenue Code.

A wholesale dealer of psychotropic substances executes a bond of Rs. 10 lakh with a surety guaranteeing compliance with storage conditions; upon breach, the dealer absconds and the entire Rs. 10 lakh is recovered from the surety by attaching the surety's agricultural land and movable property under land revenue recovery procedures.

A poppy cultivator in Madhya Pradesh who holds a government licence fails to remit the prescribed fee for the licensed acreage; the Collector, acting under the NDPS Act read with the MP Land Revenue Code, recovers the outstanding amount by treating it as revenue arrears and issuing a recovery certificate.

A company holding an import authorisation for a controlled substance under the NDPS Act defaults on fees payable; after attachment and sale of its goods yields an insufficient amount, the residual sum is recovered from the company and its directors as arrears of land revenue under State revenue law, resulting in the attachment of office premises.

A licensed opium trader in Rajasthan gives a bond for abstaining from selling to unauthorised persons; upon detection of breach, the Narcotic Commissioner initiates land-revenue-style recovery of the entire bond amount from both the trader and the named surety, leading to attachment of the surety's immovable property.
what_it_covers: Unpaid licence fees owed to the Central or State Government under the NDPS Act that remain outstanding after deduction from money owing and attachment-and-sale of goods have been attempted.

The entire sum named in a bond (other than bonds under Sections 34 and 39) executed under the NDPS Act, which becomes recoverable upon breach of the bond's conditions, from the principal or the surety.
Any other sum of any kind payable to the government under any provision of the NDPS Act or any rule or order made thereunder, where ordinary recovery modes have been exhausted or are insufficient.
Amounts recoverable from a surety who has guaranteed a licensee's or permit-holder's obligations and against whom recovery is sought as if it were land revenue arrears.
what_it_excludes: Bonds executed under Section 34 (bond for release of seized articles) and Section 39 (bond in lieu of security for bail-like purposes), which are specifically carved out and do not attract the arrears-of-land-revenue recovery mechanism under Section 72.
Fines or penalties imposed by a criminal court upon conviction under the NDPS Act, which are governed by the Code of Criminal Procedure and not by the land revenue recovery machinery.
Civil debts or contractual dues between private parties arising incidentally in the course of NDPS-regulated trade, as the provision applies only to sums payable to the Central or State Government.

Confiscated property or forfeited assets under Chapters VA and VB of the NDPS Act, which have their own distinct legal regime for attachment, freezing and forfeiture and are not recovered as land revenue arrears.
definitions.why_it_matters: The characterisation of an outstanding sum as recoverable 'as if it were arrears of land revenue' activates the swift, coercive, and court-free recovery machinery under State land revenue statutes (such as the Revenue Recovery Act, 1890, or State Land Revenue Codes), allowing the government to attach and sell immovable and movable property without filing a civil suit, significantly accelerating enforcement and creating personal liability for sureties; failure to meet these obligations can result in immediate property attachment and public auction, with no stay pending appeal unless a court specifically grants it.

definitions.definition: Arrest under the NDPS Act refers to the apprehension or taking into custody of a person by an empowered officer or pursuant to a warrant issued by a competent Magistrate, where such officer has reason to believe that the person has committed an offence punishable under the Act. Such arrest may be effected with a warrant under Section 41, without a warrant or authorisation under Section 42, or in a public place under Section 43, and must be reported to the superior officer forthwith under Section 57.
definitions.plain_english: An arrest under the NDPS Act means that an authorized government officer physically detains and takes a person into legal custody because they have good reason to believe that person has committed a drug-related crime. This can happen with or without a formal court order (warrant), depending on the situation. Once a person is arrested, the officer must report the arrest and what was seized to their senior officer as soon as possible.
real_world_examples: A Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB) officer in Mumbai, acting on a tip-off, stops and arrests a courier found carrying 500 grams of heroin concealed in a bag at Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus without a prior warrant, invoking Section 42 of the NDPS Act.

A Metropolitan Magistrate in Delhi issues a warrant of arrest against a known drug trafficker after reviewing evidence that he has been distributing psychotropic substances; police officers execute the warrant and arrest him from his residence in Rohini.

Customs officers at Chennai International Airport arrest a passenger arriving from Bangkok after discovering poppy straw concentrate hidden inside a false-bottomed suitcase, exercising arrest powers under Section 43 as it occurs in a public/transit place.

A State excise officer in Punjab, during a routine check, intercepts a vehicle on a highway and arrests the driver and occupant upon finding commercial quantities of ganja concealed beneath vegetable sacks, acting on personal knowledge and recording grounds for belief.

An officer of the Central Bureau of Narcotics in Gwalior, authorised by a gazetted officer under Section 41, arrests a licensed manufactured drug holder suspected of diverting pharmaceutical opioids into the illicit market.

Rajasthan Police arrest a foreign national near the Barmer border after receiving written information that he had smuggled opium from across the Pakistan border, and the arresting officer immediately forwards a report to his immediate official superior as required under Section 57.
what_it_covers: Apprehension by an empowered gazetted officer without a warrant when reason to believe a drug offence has been committed under Section 42.
Arrest pursuant to a warrant issued by a Metropolitan Magistrate or first-class Magistrate under Section 41 on reasonable belief of commission of an NDPS offence.
Arrest of a person found in possession of narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances in a public place or in transit by an officer of departments mentioned in Section 42, under Section 43.
Arrest authorised by a senior gazetted officer who delegates the power to a subordinate officer (above the rank of peon, sepoy, or constable) under Section 41(2).
Arrest of any person, including a licence holder for manufactured drugs, subject to the condition that the arresting officer is not below the rank of sub-inspector.
what_it_excludes: Mere detention or search of a person without formal apprehension or intent to bring them before a court or authority, which does not constitute an arrest under the Act.
Arrest by a private individual or a government official not empowered by general or special order of the Central or State Government under the NDPS Act.
Seizure of narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances alone, without the physical apprehension of a person, which constitutes seizure but not arrest.
Arrest under general criminal law (CrPC/BNSS) for offences unrelated to the NDPS Act, even if the person is also an accused in a drug matter.
Freezing or attachment of property under Chapter VA, which is a civil/preventive measure and does not amount to an arrest of the property owner.
definitions.why_it_matters: The fact of arrest under the NDPS Act triggers mandatory procedural obligations including the Section 57 report to a superior officer forthwith, determines the applicability of stringent bail conditions under Section 37, and establishes the starting point for custody, investigation, and trial timelines. Whether an arrest is lawfully effected by an empowered officer with requisite reason to believe directly impacts the admissibility of evidence seized and the validity of the entire prosecution case.

definitions.definition: "Associate" in relation to a person whose property is liable to be forfeited under this Chapter, means any individual residing or having resided in the residential premises of such person; any individual managing or having managed the affairs or kept the accounts of such person; any association of persons, body of individuals, partnership firm, or private company of which such person is or was a member, partner or director; any individual who was a member, partner or director of such entity contemporaneously with such person; any person managing the affairs or accounts of such entity; the trustee of any trust created by such person or to which such person has contributed assets amounting to not less than twenty per cent of the trust's value; or any other person whom the competent authority, for recorded reasons, considers to be holding properties on behalf of such person.
definitions.plain_english: An 'associate' is someone who is closely connected to a drug offender whose property can be seized by the government. This includes people who lived with the offender, managed their money or business, or were partners or directors in the same company. It also covers trustees of trusts set up or substantially funded by the offender, and anyone the authorities reasonably believe is holding the offender's assets on their behalf.
real_world_examples: A person named as a director of a private limited company in Mumbai alongside a drug trafficker convicted under the NDPS Act — that director qualifies as an 'associate' and their dealings with company property can be scrutinised for forfeiture.

An accountant in Delhi who has been maintaining the books of accounts and managing financial affairs of a known narcotics smuggler is treated as an 'associate', making properties in the accountant's name potentially liable to inquiry under Chapter VA.

A cousin living in the same residential bungalow in Chennai as a person arrested for trafficking in commercial quantities of heroin is classified as an 'associate', allowing the competent authority to examine whether any property held by the cousin actually belongs to the accused.

A trust registered in Kolkata, created by a person convicted of operating a drug cartel, whose trustee holds real estate funded primarily by that convicted person's contributions (exceeding 20% of trust assets) — the trustee is an 'associate' and the trust property is subject to forfeiture proceedings.

A business partner in a partnership firm based in Ahmedabad, who was a partner simultaneously with a person detained under the Prevention of Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1988, is an 'associate' whose share in firm assets can be investigated.

A former flat-mate who lived in the residential premises of a convicted drug offender in Hyderabad during the period of the offence is classified as an 'associate', enabling the competent authority to probe whether any property ostensibly belonging to that flat-mate is actually the offender's concealed asset.
what_it_covers: Any individual who currently or previously resided in the residential premises (including outhouses) of the drug offender whose property is subject to forfeiture.
Any individual who manages or has managed the financial affairs or accounts of the drug offender.

Any association of persons, body of individuals, partnership firm, or private company (within the meaning of the Companies Act, 1956) of which the drug offender is or was a member, partner, or director.
Any individual who was simultaneously a member, partner, or director of the same corporate or associative body as the drug offender at the relevant time.

The trustee of a trust created by the drug offender, or a trust in which the drug offender's contributions constitute at least twenty per cent of the trust's total asset value on the date of contribution.
Any other person whom the competent authority, after recording written reasons, believes is holding properties of the drug offender on that person's behalf.
what_it_excludes: A transferee in good faith for adequate consideration who acquired property from the drug offender without knowledge of its illicit origin is not treated as an associate merely by virtue of that transaction.

A mere acquaintance, friend, or social contact of the drug offender who neither resided in the offender's premises, nor managed their affairs, nor shared a formal business or trust relationship does not fall within the definition.

A person who is a relative (as separately defined under the Act) is categorised under the specific 'relative' clause of Section 68A and is not subsumed within the definition of 'associate', though both categories may attract similar consequences.

A public or listed company (not being a private company within the meaning of the Companies Act, 1956) in which the drug offender holds shares as an ordinary investor is not itself an 'associate' under the sub-clause referring to private companies and partnerships.

An individual who managed the affairs of an entity but did so at a time when the drug offender was not a member, partner, or director of that entity is not covered as an associate under sub-clause (v) of the definition.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as an 'associate' under Section 68B determines whether that person falls within the scope of Chapter VA of the NDPS Act, making their property liable to forfeiture as 'illegally acquired property' and subjecting them to proceedings before the competent authority and the Appellate Tribunal. The classification as an associate directly triggers the burden of demonstrating that properties held by them are not illegally acquired, and failure to do so can result in forfeiture of those properties to the Central Government.

definitions.definition: Authorisation is not expressly defined in Section 2 of the NDPS Act, 1985, but is used throughout the Act to denote an official written permission or sanction issued by a competent authority under the Act or rules framed thereunder, enabling a person or entity to lawfully engage in activities involving narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances that would otherwise constitute an offence under the Act.
definitions.plain_english: An 'authorisation' is an official government permission that allows a person, organisation, or business to legally deal with narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances in specific ways — such as manufacturing, selling, transporting, or using them for medical or scientific purposes. Without this permission, the same activities would be treated as serious criminal offences. Think of it as a special licence or clearance given by the government to ensure that any handling of dangerous drugs happens only for legitimate, regulated purposes.
real_world_examples: A pharmaceutical company in Hyderabad obtains an authorisation from the Narcotics Commissioner to manufacture codeine-based cough syrups for medicinal use, allowing it to legally procure opium derivatives from licensed sources.

A government hospital in Mumbai applies for and receives an authorisation from the State Drug Controller to stock and administer morphine injections to cancer patients under palliative care, thereby exempting the hospital from the general prohibition under Section 8.

A research institution in Pune is granted an authorisation by the Central Government to import small quantities of a psychotropic substance for scientific study, shielding its scientists from prosecution under the NDPS Act.

A licensed exporter in Delhi receives an authorisation under Section 24 to export poppy straw concentrate to a foreign pharmaceutical buyer in Germany, allowing the consignment to pass through customs legally.

A state government factory in Ghaziabad operating under Central Government ownership is given an authorisation to cultivate opium poppy and process medicinal opium for domestic pharmaceutical supply, distinguishing its operations from illicit cultivation.

An enforcement officer under Section 50A is duly authorised to conduct a controlled delivery operation, allowing a suspect consignment of heroin to pass through Mumbai port under surveillance to identify the organised criminal network behind the trafficking.
what_it_covers: Written permission issued by the Central Government or a notified authority allowing manufacture, sale, transport, import, or export of narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances for medical or scientific purposes.
Authorisation granted to enforcement officers under Section 50A enabling them to carry out controlled delivery operations involving illicit consignments of narcotic or psychotropic substances.
Permission issued under rules framed under the NDPS Act to licensed pharmaceutical entities, hospitals, or research institutions to possess or use controlled substances within prescribed limits.
Conditions attached to a licence or permit that together constitute an 'authorisation' for purposes of the illicit traffic definition, distinguishing regulated activity from criminal conduct.
Authorisation granted to Central Government factories for the cultivation, production, or processing of opium and its derivatives for lawful domestic pharmaceutical supply.
what_it_excludes: Informal or verbal permissions from officials, which carry no legal standing as an 'authorisation' under the Act and do not protect a person from prosecution.
Licences or permits issued under other laws such as the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, unless specifically recognised or cross-referenced under the NDPS Act or its rules.
Authorisations obtained through fraud, misrepresentation, or bribery, which are void and cannot be used as a defence against charges of illicit traffic or contravention.

General professional credentials of doctors or pharmacists, which do not by themselves constitute an 'authorisation' to deal in narcotic drugs beyond the specific permissions granted under NDPS rules.

Activities carried out in excess of the scope, quantity, or geographical limits specified in the authorisation, which remain unlawful even if a valid authorisation exists for other aspects of the activity.
definitions.why_it_matters: The presence or absence of a valid authorisation is the critical legal dividing line between a lawful regulated activity and a criminal offence under Sections 8, 24, 26, and 32 of the NDPS Act — without it, dealings in narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances attract severe penalties including rigorous imprisonment of up to 20 years and heavy fines; conversely, a valid authorisation provides a complete legal defence against prosecution for the specifically permitted activity.

definitions.definition: An authorisation of arrest is a formal written authorisation issued by a competent officer or authority under the NDPS Act empowering the arrest of a person suspected of committing an offence punishable under the Act with imprisonment for a term of ten years or more, or a similar offence under any corresponding law of any other country. It functions analogously to a warrant of arrest but is issued by an empowered officer rather than a court, and its issuance brings the subject person within the scope of Chapter VA provisions relating to illegally acquired property.
definitions.plain_english: An authorisation of arrest is an official document issued by a designated drug enforcement officer giving permission to arrest a person suspected of a serious drug offence under the NDPS Act. Unlike a court warrant, it is issued by an authorised officer rather than a judge. Once such an authorisation is issued against a person, they and their property come under the scrutiny of special laws dealing with drug-related illegal wealth. If the authorisation is later withdrawn, any property seized or frozen on that basis must be released.
real_world_examples: A Narcotics Control Bureau officer in Mumbai issues an authorisation of arrest against a suspected drug trafficker believed to be involved in large-scale heroin smuggling punishable with ten years or more imprisonment — this immediately subjects the accused and their family members to Chapter VA property forfeiture provisions.

An NCB officer in Delhi issues an authorisation of arrest against an individual linked to an international narcotics syndicate operating across India and Afghanistan; the issuance triggers the six-year lookback period under Section 68C for identifying illegally acquired properties.

A gazetted officer of the Customs Department issues an authorisation of arrest against a person in Chennai suspected of large-scale psychotropic substance trafficking; the accused's associates and relatives become liable to have their properties examined under Chapter VA.

In Kolkata, an authorisation of arrest is issued against a person suspected of financing a major cannabis smuggling operation; when the authorisation is later withdrawn after the person is acquitted, Section 68Z mandates that all seized and frozen properties of that person be released.

An empowered officer under the NDPS Act issues an authorisation of arrest against a foreign national suspected of trafficking opium derivatives into India in quantities attracting ten or more years imprisonment, bringing the person within the scope of Section 68A(2)(cc) as one against whom such authorisation has been issued.
what_it_covers: A written authorisation issued by an empowered NDPS officer against a person suspected of an offence under the NDPS Act carrying imprisonment of ten years or more.
An authorisation issued against a person suspected of a similar offence under any corresponding law of any other country.
The document that, once issued, brings the subject and their relatives, associates, and property holders within the ambit of Chapter VA forfeiture provisions.
The authorisation whose issuance sets the start point of the six-year lookback period for computing illegally acquired property under Section 68C.
An authorisation that, if withdrawn following acquittal or discharge, mandates the release of all seized or frozen property under Section 68Z.
what_it_excludes: A court-issued warrant of arrest, which is a distinct instrument issued by a Magistrate or Special Court rather than an empowered officer.
Arrest authorisations issued for NDPS offences carrying less than ten years of imprisonment, which do not bring a person within Chapter VA.
Detention orders issued under the Prevention of Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1988, which are a separate category under Section 68A(2)(b).
Summons or notices issued to persons for inquiry or investigation that do not authorise physical arrest.
Authorisations issued for offences unrelated to narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances, even if issued by the same enforcement officer.
definitions.why_it_matters: The issuance of an authorisation of arrest is a threshold event under Chapter VA of the NDPS Act: it determines whether a person (and their relatives, associates, and property holders) falls within the scope of the illegally acquired property forfeiture regime and sets the six-year lookback period for identifying such property. Conversely, the withdrawal of an authorisation of arrest following acquittal or discharge directly triggers the mandatory release of all seized and frozen properties under Section 68Z.

definitions.definition: An 'authority' under the NDPS Act refers to any authority or hierarchy of authorities constituted by the Central Government by order published in the Official Gazette under Section 4(3) for the purpose of exercising such powers and functions of the Central Government under this Act as may be specified in the order, including powers of superintendence, coordination, and enforcement; it also includes, contextually, any governmental body, officer, or institutional entity empowered under this Act or directed by the Central Government or State Government to exercise control, direction, or regulatory functions in relation to narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances.
definitions.plain_english: An 'authority' is any government body or official entity set up or recognised under the NDPS Act to carry out specific duties related to controlling narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances. The Central Government can create such an authority by a gazette notification and give it specific powers to act on the government's behalf. This includes bodies like the Narcotics Control Bureau or any hierarchy of officials tasked with enforcement, regulation, or coordination under the Act.
real_world_examples: The Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB), constituted by the Central Government under the NDPS Act, acts as an 'authority' empowered to investigate and coordinate drug-related offences across India, such as when it conducts raids on drug trafficking networks in Mumbai or Delhi.

A State Government-constituted excise authority in Rajasthan that is specifically empowered to regulate and supervise the licensed cultivation of opium poppy in designated areas functions as an 'authority' under the Act.

When the Central Government issues a gazette notification constituting a Special Task Force with defined powers to intercept and seize psychotropic substances at international airports like Indira Gandhi International Airport, that Task Force qualifies as an 'authority' under Section 4(3).

Under Section 73 of the NDPS Act, when a customs officer at Chennai Port arrests a smuggler and forwards the case to the empowered 'authority' for further action and reporting, the receiving body—whether the NCB regional unit or a designated officer hierarchy—acts as the 'authority' for that purpose.

A district-level narcotic cell constituted under State Government direction and vested with powers to grant or cancel permits for medicinal opium distribution in Madhya Pradesh operates as an 'authority' within the meaning of the Act.
what_it_covers: The Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB) constituted by the Central Government under Section 4(3) with specific powers to enforce the NDPS Act.
Any hierarchy of officers or bodies formally created by a Central Government gazette notification and vested with delegated powers and functions under the NDPS Act.
State Government-designated bodies such as excise authorities or narcotics cells empowered to regulate, supervise, or take enforcement action under the NDPS Act.
Authorities receiving arrest reports or case documents under Section 73, such as a regional NCB unit or designated superior officer hierarchy.
International coordination bodies or mechanisms recognised by the Central Government for purposes of fulfilling India's obligations under International Conventions on narcotic drugs.
what_it_excludes: Private individuals or non-governmental organisations, even if involved in drug rehabilitation or awareness, as they are not constituted by government order under this Act.
Ordinary police officers acting in their general capacity under the Code of Criminal Procedure who have not been specifically empowered or designated under the NDPS Act.
Judicial bodies such as Special Courts or the High Court, which are distinct from 'authorities' and exercise judicial rather than executive or regulatory functions under the Act.
An officer acting purely in a personal or unofficial capacity, without a formal order or direction from Central or State Government vesting authority under this Act.
Foreign law enforcement agencies or Interpol, which may cooperate with Indian authorities but are not themselves 'authorities' constituted under the NDPS Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: The determination of whether a body qualifies as an 'authority' under the NDPS Act directly governs whether its actions—such as arrests, seizures, searches, and regulatory orders—are legally valid and enforceable; actions taken by an unauthorised or improperly constituted body may be challenged as without jurisdiction, rendering arrests, seizures, or prosecutions under provisions like Section 73 legally defective.

Examples: The Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB), constituted by the Central Government under the NDPS Act, acts as an 'authority' empowered to investigate and coordinate drug-related offences across India, such as when it conducts raids on drug trafficking networks in Mumbai or Delhi. | A State Government-constituted excise authority in Rajasthan that is specifically empowered to regulate and supervise the licensed cultivation of opium poppy in designated areas functions as an 'authority' under the Act. | When the Central Government issues a gazette notification constituting a Special Task Force with defined powers to intercept and seize psychotropic substances at international airports like Indira Gandhi International Airport, that Task Force qualifies as an 'authority' under Section 4(3). | Under Section 73 of the NDPS Act, when a customs officer at Chennai Port arrests a smuggler and forwards the case to the empowered 'authority' for further action and reporting, the receiving body—whether the NCB regional unit or a designated officer hierarchy—acts as the 'authority' for that purpose. | A district-level narcotic cell constituted under State Government direction and vested with powers to grant or cancel permits for medicinal opium distribution in Madhya Pradesh operates as an 'authority' within the meaning of the Act.

definitions.definition: As used in Section 35 of the NDPS Act, 'belief' is a component of 'culpable mental state' and refers to a person's subjective acceptance or conviction that a particular fact exists, as distinguished from mere suspicion or conjecture; it includes 'reason to believe' a fact and is presumed by the court in prosecutions requiring a culpable mental state, unless the accused proves its absence beyond a preponderance of probability.
definitions.plain_english: Belief means that a person genuinely accepts or is convinced that a certain fact is true — for example, that a substance is a narcotic drug. In NDPS cases, the court automatically assumes that an accused had this belief when they are charged with an offence that requires a guilty state of mind. The accused must then prove they did NOT have such a belief in order to escape liability.
real_world_examples: A drug courier arrested at Delhi airport with heroin-filled packets is presumed by the court to have believed the packets contained a narcotic drug, unless he can prove he genuinely thought it was a food item placed by a stranger without his knowledge.

A warehouse owner in Mumbai whose godown is found storing seized psychotropic substances is presumed to have believed in the existence of those substances on his premises; he must lead evidence showing he had no actual awareness or conviction about what was stored.

A truck driver in Rajasthan transporting cannabis hidden beneath sacks of grain is presumed under Section 35 to have held a belief that the contraband was present; his defence that he was unloaded cargo blindly without any knowledge will be tested against this presumption.

An accused pharmacist in Chennai who supplies controlled substances without a valid prescription is presumed to have believed he was engaging in an unauthorised transaction; he must establish to the court's satisfaction that he had no such conviction.

A person found financing a narcotics operation in Punjab is presumed to have believed that the money was being used for illicit drug trafficking, and must positively disprove that belief to avail himself of a defence under the NDPS Act.
what_it_covers: A person's subjective conviction that a substance in their possession is a narcotic drug or psychotropic substance, even if not confirmed by scientific testing at the time of possession.

An accused's acceptance or awareness that a particular fact (such as the illicit nature of goods being transported) exists, which is presumed by the court once the prosecution establishes the actus reus.

Reason to believe a fact, which is explicitly included within 'belief' under Section 35, covering situations where the accused had sufficient grounds or information to form a conviction about the existence of a fact.
Belief formed on the basis of circumstantial information, such as being told by an associate that a parcel contains contraband, which is sufficient to attract the presumption under Section 35.
what_it_excludes: Mere suspicion or vague apprehension that a fact might exist, which does not amount to 'belief' and is insufficient to establish the culpable mental state required for conviction.
Mistaken belief genuinely held by the accused in good faith and supported by credible evidence, which can serve as a defence to rebut the statutory presumption under Section 35.
Belief formed after the commission of the offence, as Section 35 is concerned only with the mental state existing at the time the offending act was committed.
Constructive or imputed belief based solely on the accused's status or position without any factual basis or information linking them to knowledge of the narcotic substance.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an accused is found to have held a 'belief' regarding the relevant fact directly determines the existence of culpable mental state, which is an essential ingredient of most offences under the NDPS Act; if the presumption of belief stands unrebutted, the accused faces conviction and the severe penalties prescribed under the Act, whereas a successful rebuttal can result in acquittal. The term also controls the admissibility and weight of a defence plea, since the accused bears the reverse burden of disproving belief to the court's satisfaction under Section 35.

definitions.definition: "Board" means the Central Board of Excise and Customs constituted under the Central Boards of Revenue Act, 1963 (54 of 1963).
definitions.plain_english: The 'Board' refers to the Central Board of Excise and Customs (CBEC), which is the top government body in India that oversees customs and excise administration. It was created under a specific law from 1963 called the Central Boards of Revenue Act. Under the NDPS Act, this body holds significant supervisory and regulatory authority over matters relating to narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances at customs and excise checkpoints.
real_world_examples: When a consignment of suspected heroin is intercepted at the Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust in Mumbai by Customs officers, the Central Board of Excise and Customs (Board) exercises supervisory authority over the investigation and seizure proceedings under the NDPS Act.

The Board issues instructions and guidelines to Customs officers posted at international airports like Indira Gandhi International Airport, Delhi, enabling them to conduct searches, inspections, and seizures of narcotic drugs under Section 42 and related provisions of the NDPS Act.

When a licensed opium dealer is suspected of diverting government-allotted opium for illicit trade, the Board, through its field officers, can initiate inquiry and enforcement proceedings under the NDPS Act to regulate Central Government factories and licensed operations.

At the Attari-Wagah land border crossing between India and Pakistan, Customs officials operating under the Board's jurisdiction intercept psychotropic substances being smuggled in commercial goods consignments, invoking powers granted to them under the NDPS Act.

The Board coordinates with the Narcotics Control Bureau in controlled delivery operations at sea ports and air cargo terminals to allow suspect narcotic consignments to pass through Indian territory under supervision, as permitted under the NDPS Act.
what_it_covers: The Central Board of Excise and Customs constituted specifically under the Central Boards of Revenue Act, 1963 (54 of 1963) as the authoritative body.

All functions, powers, and responsibilities assigned to the Board under Sections 2, 5, and 75 of the NDPS Act, including supervisory authority over narcotic drug and psychotropic substance matters at customs and excise levels.
Customs and excise officers functioning under the Board's jurisdiction who are empowered to enforce NDPS provisions at ports, airports, land borders, and inland check-posts across India.
Policy directions, circulars, and instructions issued by the Board to field officers for implementing the NDPS Act's provisions relating to import, export, and transit of controlled substances.
what_it_excludes: The Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT), which is a separate board under the Central Boards of Revenue Act and has no role under the NDPS Act.
State-level excise boards or state excise departments, which are constituted under respective State Acts and are not the 'Board' as defined under the NDPS Act.
The Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB) and the Narcotics Commissioner, which are separate statutory bodies under the NDPS Act with distinct roles and are not subsumed within the definition of 'Board'.
Any ad hoc committees, task forces, or advisory panels set up by the Central Government for drug policy that are not the formally constituted Central Board of Excise and Customs under the 1963 Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: The precise identification of the 'Board' determines which authority has legal jurisdiction to issue licences, permits, and authorisations under Section 5 and to receive reports or exercise oversight functions under Section 75 of the NDPS Act; actions taken by any other body purporting to act as the 'Board' would lack statutory validity and could render enforcement actions, seizures, or prosecutions legally infirm.

definitions.definition: A bond, within the NDPS Act, is a written undertaking executed by an accused or convicted person, with or without sureties, binding such person to abstain from the commission of any offence under Chapter IV of the Act for a specified period, or to appear before the court as directed, in a form prescribed by the Central Government and governed by the applicable provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
definitions.plain_english: A bond is a formal written promise made by a person to the court, guaranteeing that they will follow certain conditions — such as not committing drug-related offences again, or appearing before the court when required. It may be backed by one or more guarantors (sureties) who also sign and are financially liable if the person breaks the promise. If the person violates the bond conditions, they can be brought back before the court to face consequences.
real_world_examples: A person convicted under Section 27 of the NDPS Act for personal consumption of a small quantity of heroin is released on probation by a Mumbai sessions court. The court orders him to execute a bond of Rs. 10,000 with one surety, committing to undergo de-addiction treatment at a government-recognised centre in Pune and to abstain from drug offences for two years.

An addict found guilty of possessing a small quantity of cannabis in Delhi is directed by the court under Section 39 to enter into a bond without surety, agreeing to appear before the court within one year with a medical report from AIIMS confirming completion of de-toxification treatment.

A repeat offender convicted for manufacturing a psychotropic substance in Gujarat is sentenced to imprisonment, and the court additionally orders him to execute a security bond of Rs. 50,000 with two sureties under Section 34, binding him not to commit any NDPS offence for three years after his release.

Before the Special Court in Chennai hearing an NDPS case, bail is granted to an accused charged with importing cocaine into India; the court applies CrPC provisions (as extended by Section 36C) requiring the accused to execute a bail bond of Rs. 2,00,000 with two local sureties as a condition of release pending trial.

An appellate court in Kolkata, while hearing an appeal against a conviction for ganja trafficking, modifies the sentence and additionally directs the appellant to execute a bond for Rs. 25,000 under Section 34, enforceable for one year, as a condition tied to the modified order.

A person accused of financing illicit drug trafficking is granted bail by the High Court under Section 37, subject to executing a personal bond of Rs. 5,00,000 along with two solvent sureties to ensure appearance at each date of hearing before the Special Court.
what_it_covers: A bond executed by a convicted person under Section 34 binding them not to commit any Chapter IV offence for a period up to three years, with or without sureties, in the form prescribed by the Central Government.

A bond entered into by an addict under Section 39 as a condition for release on probation, committing to undergo de-addiction treatment and appear before the court with a medical report within one year.

Bail bonds executed under Section 36C before a Special Court, where the CrPC provisions on bail and bonds apply and the accused furnishes a personal bond with or without sureties to secure their appearance during trial.
A bond ordered by an appellate court or the High Court or Sessions Judge exercising revisional powers under Section 34 as part of a modified sentence or order.
A bond executed by a released addict under Section 39(2) for abstaining from Chapter IV offences for up to three years after completion of medical treatment.
what_it_excludes: Mere verbal or informal assurances given by an accused to police or investigating officers, which do not constitute a bond in the legal sense under the Act.
Civil contractual bonds or financial instruments (such as surety bonds in commercial transactions) unrelated to criminal proceedings under the NDPS Act.

Undertakings or recognisances executed solely in the context of other statutes (e.g., the Customs Act or the Prevention of Money Laundering Act) that are not specifically ordered under the NDPS Act's framework.
Cases where a conviction under Chapter IV is set aside on appeal or in revision — the bond executed automatically becomes void and ceases to have any legal effect.
Bonds executed under Section 106 of the CrPC for keeping the peace in non-NDPS matters, even though the NDPS Act uses that section as a reference template for procedural purposes.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a bond is properly executed determines if an accused or convicted person can be lawfully released on probation or bail under the NDPS Act, and breach of the bond's conditions empowers the court to recall the person, forfeit the bond amount, and impose the original or enhanced sentence. The existence of a valid bond is a prerequisite for courts to exercise their discretionary power to release addicts on probation under Section 39 or to impose post-conviction security under Section 34.

definitions.definition: "cannabis (hemp)" means— charas, that is, the separated resin, in whatever form, whether crude or purified, obtained from the cannabis plant and also includes concentrated preparation and resin known as hashish oil or liquid hashish; ganja, that is, the flowering or fruiting tops of the cannabis plant (excluding the seeds and leaves when not accompanied by the tops), by whatever name they may be known or designated; and any mixture, with or without any neutral material, of any of the above forms of cannabis or any drink prepared therefrom.
definitions.plain_english: Cannabis under this law covers three things: charas (the sticky resin scraped from the cannabis plant, including hashish oil), ganja (the flowering or fruiting tops of the cannabis plant, but not plain seeds or leaves on their own), and any mixture or drink made from either of these. Essentially, it covers the most commonly abused forms of the cannabis plant in India. Plain leaves and seeds by themselves are not included unless they come with the tops of the plant.
real_world_examples: A person in Himachal Pradesh found in possession of hand-rubbed charas (resin) collected from cannabis plants grown in the Kullu valley is in possession of 'cannabis' under the NDPS Act and can be prosecuted under Section 20.
A drug peddler in Mumbai caught selling ganja — dried flowering tops of the cannabis plant — to college students is trafficking 'cannabis' and is liable for offences under Section 20 of the NDPS Act.

A roadside vendor in Kerala selling bhang (a drink prepared from cannabis leaves and tops) mixed with other ingredients is selling a 'drink prepared from cannabis' and the product qualifies as cannabis under the Act.

Customs officers at Chennai airport intercepting a parcel containing hashish oil (liquid hashish) imported from abroad are seizing 'cannabis' in the form of charas concentrate, triggering prosecution under Sections 20 and relevant import provisions of the NDPS Act.

A rave party organiser in Goa where attendees are found consuming hash brownies — baked goods made with cannabis resin — is facilitating consumption of 'cannabis' as a mixture containing charas, attracting NDPS liability.

Police in Rajasthan discovering a large consignment of dried ganja being transported in a truck hidden under agricultural produce are seizing 'cannabis' under the NDPS Act, with quantity determining whether it constitutes small, intermediate, or commercial quantity.
what_it_covers: Charas — the separated resin of the cannabis plant in any form, whether crude or purified, including hashish oil and liquid hashish.
Ganja — the flowering or fruiting tops of the cannabis plant, by whatever name called, even when accompanied by seeds and leaves.
Any mixture of charas or ganja with or without neutral material, including drinks such as bhang prepared from these forms of cannabis.
Concentrated cannabis resin preparations such as hash cakes or edibles that contain charas or ganja as an ingredient.
Hashish oil or liquid hashish, which is a concentrated extract of cannabis resin.
what_it_excludes: Seeds of the cannabis plant when not accompanied by the flowering or fruiting tops.
Leaves of the cannabis plant when not accompanied by the flowering or fruiting tops.
The cannabis plant itself in its live, growing form — which is separately defined as 'cannabis plant' (genus cannabis) and governed by cultivation provisions.
Medicinal cannabis, which is a separately defined term under the Act and falls under the category of 'manufactured drug' with a distinct regulatory regime.
Industrial hemp products such as hemp fibre or hemp seed oil used for non-psychoactive commercial purposes, to the extent they do not contain charas or ganja as defined.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a substance qualifies as 'cannabis' under the NDPS Act directly determines whether possession, sale, transport, or cultivation attracts criminal liability under Section 20 (which prescribes rigorous imprisonment up to 10 years for small quantity and up to 20 years for commercial quantity). The classification also determines the applicable quantity thresholds for 'small quantity' and 'commercial quantity' notifications, which govern the severity of punishment.

definitions.plain_english: A cannabis plant refers to any plant that belongs to the botanical genus Cannabis, regardless of its species, variety, or strain. The definition is intentionally broad so that no variety of the cannabis genus escapes regulation under the law.
