definitions.definition: "International Convention" means the Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs, 1961 adopted by the United Nations Conference at New York in March, 1961; the Protocol amending that Convention adopted by the United Nations Conference at Geneva in March, 1972; the Convention on Psychotropic Substances, 1971 adopted by the United Nations Conference at Vienna in February, 1971; and any other international convention, or protocol or other instrument amending an international convention, relating to narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances which may be ratified or acceded to by India after the commencement of this Act.
definitions.plain_english: An 'International Convention' refers to specific global treaties and agreements on controlling narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances that India has agreed to follow. These include two major United Nations treaties from 1961 and 1971, their amending protocols, and any future international drug-related treaties that India formally joins. Essentially, it is the set of international rules that India has committed to uphold in its fight against drug trafficking and abuse.
real_world_examples: When the Central Government considers whether to classify a new synthetic opioid (such as tramadol analogues) as a 'controlled substance' under the NDPS Act, it refers to decisions taken under the Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs, 1961 — an International Convention — to determine whether the substance should be scheduled and regulated.

India ratified the United Nations Convention Against Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances, 1988. Once acceded to, this treaty qualifies as an International Convention under the NDPS Act, enabling Indian courts and agencies to align domestic enforcement with its obligations, such as allowing controlled delivery operations.

The Narcotics Control Bureau relies on the Convention on Psychotropic Substances, 1971 (an International Convention) to justify placing substances like MDMA and LSD under Schedule I of the NDPS Act, ensuring India's scheduling decisions mirror international obligations.

When the Central Government issues a notification in the Official Gazette declaring a new precursor chemical (e.g., a new ephedrine derivative) as a 'controlled substance,' it expressly relies on provisions of the relevant International Convention to legally justify the classification, giving the notification a stronger statutory foundation.

A pharmaceutical company seeking to import a newly developed psychoactive compound challenges its classification as a psychotropic substance. definitions.definition: Investigation, as used under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, refers to the process of inquiry, examination, collection of evidence, and all procedural steps undertaken by an officer empowered under Section 53 or an officer-in-charge of a police station to ascertain the facts and circumstances constituting an offence under the Act, including search, seizure, arrest, recording of statements, and gathering of documents, culminating in the filing of a police report before the Special Court. The term encompasses the entire procedural journey from the point of detection or suspicion of an offence to the submission of the charge sheet.
definitions.plain_english: Investigation under the NDPS Act means the official process by which authorised government officers — such as narcotics officers, customs officers, or police — look into whether a drug-related crime has been committed. This includes searching places, seizing drugs or documents, arresting suspects, and recording statements to build a case. The investigation starts when an officer suspects an offence and ends when a report is submitted to the Special Court for trial.
real_world_examples: A Narcotics Control Bureau officer at Indira Gandhi International Airport, Delhi, suspects a passenger carrying heroin concealed in luggage; the officer initiates investigation by detaining the passenger, seizing the contraband, recording statements, and submitting a charge sheet to the Special Court — all steps forming part of the investigation.

A Central Excise and Narcotics officer in Manali, Himachal Pradesh, receives a tip-off about illicit cultivation of cannabis; the officer conducts field searches, seizes plants, collects soil and forensic samples, interrogates the occupier of land, and documents findings as part of the investigation under the NDPS Act.

A Customs officer at Chennai Port intercepts a container with concealed pseudoephedrine; the officer invests powers under Section 53, conducts a panchnama, seizes the controlled substance, records statements of the importer and shipping agent, and forwards the accused to the Special Court — constituting the full investigation.

A State Excise officer in Rajasthan, empowered under Section 53, investigates illicit opium trade by conducting surveillance, performing test purchases, arresting the accused, seizing opium and financial records, and gathering witness testimony before filing a police report with the Special Court.

In a case involving commercial quantity of methamphetamine in Mumbai, the Narcotics Control Bureau conducts prolonged investigation over 180 days involving bank record analysis, mobile surveillance, and cross-border coordination, applying to the Special Court under Section 36A for an extension of detention due to complexity of the investigation.
what_it_covers: Search of persons, premises, vehicles, and conveyances suspected of involvement in drug offences by officers empowered under Section 53.
Seizure of narcotic drugs, psychotropic substances, documents, and property connected to the alleged offence.
Recording of statements by empowered officers under Section 53A and interrogation of suspects, accused, and witnesses.
Arrest of persons suspected of committing offences under the NDPS Act and their production before a Magistrate or Special Court.
Collection, preservation, and forensic analysis of seized substances and documents as evidence.
Filing of a police report or charge sheet before the Special Court upon conclusion of the investigation.
what_it_excludes: Trial proceedings before the Special Court, which commence after the investigation concludes and the charge sheet is filed.
Purely administrative departmental inquiries conducted by government agencies that do not relate to offences under the NDPS Act.
Proceedings before the Appellate Tribunal or civil forfeiture proceedings under Chapter VA, which are adjudicatory in nature and distinct from criminal investigation.
Preliminary intelligence gathering or surveillance activity conducted before any formal suspicion of a specific offence arises and before statutory powers are invoked.
Action taken under other laws (such as Customs Act or IPC) where no offence under the NDPS Act is being investigated, even if drugs are incidentally involved.
definitions.why_it_matters: The determination of whether an 'investigation' under the NDPS Act is properly conducted by an officer empowered under Section 53 directly governs the admissibility of evidence, including statements recorded under Section 53A, and the legality of search, seizure, and arrest; any procedural defect in investigation can result in acquittal or discharge of the accused before the Special Court. Additionally, the duration and progress of investigation triggers the Special Court's power under Section 36A to extend detention beyond 180 days, making the integrity and timeliness of investigation a critical safeguard against arbitrary detention.

definitions.definition: Under Section 35 of the NDPS Act, 'knowledge' is a culpable mental state that is presumed to exist when an accused person is in possession of a narcotic drug, psychotropic substance, or other article in respect of which an offence has been committed, unless the accused proves to the court's satisfaction that he had no such knowledge. The court may presume the existence of such knowledge from the facts and circumstances of each case.
definitions.plain_english: Knowledge, in the context of the NDPS Act, means being aware that what you possess or deal with is a narcotic drug, psychotropic substance, or contraband covered by the law. If police find you with such a substance, the law automatically assumes you knew what it was — it is then your job to prove in court that you genuinely did not know. This reversal of the usual burden of proof makes it very difficult to claim ignorance as a defence.
real_world_examples: A courier from Mumbai is intercepted at Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport carrying a bag containing concealed packets of heroin. Even though he claims a stranger asked him to carry the bag, the court presumes he had knowledge of the contraband under Section 35, and he must prove his lack of awareness.

A truck driver in Punjab is found transporting a consignment that, along with legitimate goods, contains hidden pouches of cannabis. He claims ignorance of the hidden pouches. Under the NDPS Act, his physical possession raises a presumption of knowledge, which he must rebut with evidence.

A lodger in a Delhi flat is arrested when police recover methamphetamine from the premises. Although he argues the drugs belonged to his roommate, the court presumes his knowledge of the substance present in his shared residence, and he must lead evidence to the contrary.

A person at a Goa beach party is found holding a small packet of MDMA (ecstasy). She claims someone handed it to her moments before police arrived and she did not know its contents. Section 35 presumes she had knowledge of the psychotropic nature of the substance she was holding.

A pharmacist in Hyderabad is caught selling codeine-based preparations in quantities exceeding permissible limits without valid prescriptions. The court presumes he had knowledge that such excess supply was an offence under the NDPS Act, placing on him the burden to prove he was unaware of the restriction.
what_it_covers: Awareness that a substance in one's possession is a narcotic drug or psychotropic substance prohibited or regulated under the NDPS Act.
Constructive knowledge inferred from circumstances — such as concealment of drugs in luggage, hidden compartments in vehicles, or coded language in communications — even without direct admission.
Knowledge of the illicit nature of a transaction, such as knowingly financing or facilitating the transportation of narcotic drugs across state or national borders.
Awareness by a premises owner or occupier that the premises are being used for storage or sale of narcotic drugs, making him liable for harbouring such activities.
Knowledge imputed to an accused in a controlled delivery operation where the accused is observed to be a conscious participant in the movement of contraband.
what_it_excludes: Genuine and provable ignorance of the narcotic or psychotropic nature of a substance — for example, where a person can conclusively demonstrate they were deceived or misled about the contents of a parcel they carried.

Accidental or unknowing physical proximity to drugs without any element of possession, control, or participation — such as a bystander present at a location where drugs are seized but having no connection to them.

Knowledge that cannot be legally presumed in the absence of any incriminating circumstances connecting the accused to the narcotic substance, e.g., where a person is merely a visitor with no link to the contraband found on someone else's property.
Situations where the substance is a legally authorised and licensed preparation and the person deals with it within the bounds of a valid permit or authorisation under the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Under Section 35 of the NDPS Act, once possession of a narcotic drug or psychotropic substance is established, knowledge is statutorily presumed against the accused, shifting the burden of proof onto the defence — failure to rebut this presumption leads to conviction for offences such as possession, sale, or transportation under Sections 20, 21, 22, and 29. The presence or absence of knowledge thus directly determines criminal liability, the severity of punishment, and whether enhanced penalties for commercial quantities apply.

definitions.definition: The term 'licence' is not expressly defined in Section 2 of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985; however, as used throughout the Act, a 'licence' means a formal written permission or authorisation granted by a competent government authority permitting a person, firm, or entity to lawfully cultivate, produce, manufacture, possess, sell, purchase, transport, or otherwise deal in narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances in accordance with the conditions specified therein. Such a licence is a prerequisite to engage in any activity involving narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances that would otherwise constitute an offence under the Act.
definitions.plain_english: A licence under the NDPS Act is an official permit issued by the government that legally allows a person or business to handle controlled substances like narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances. Without this permit, handling such substances is a criminal offence. The licence comes with specific rules and conditions that the holder must follow at all times.
real_world_examples: A pharmaceutical company in Hyderabad applies to the Narcotics Commissioner and obtains a licence to manufacture codeine-based cough syrups, allowing it to legally purchase opium derivatives from licensed suppliers and produce the medication within permitted quantities.

A government-approved poppy cultivator in Madhya Pradesh is granted a licence by the state government under NDPS rules to cultivate opium poppy on a specified area of land for a particular crop season, and must surrender the entire harvest to government collection centres.

A licensed pharmacist in Mumbai holding a valid licence under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act read with NDPS rules is permitted to stock and dispense Schedule X psychotropic substances such as diazepam only against valid medical prescriptions, subject to record-keeping requirements.

A Central Government factory in Ghaziabad (such as the Government Opium and Alkaloid Works) operates under a licence issued by the Central Government to manufacture medicinal opium and opium derivatives like morphine for export and domestic medical supply.

An importer in Delhi obtains a licence from the relevant authority to import a psychotropic substance listed under the NDPS Act for use in a research institution, subject to conditions specifying quantity, end-use, and storage requirements.

A hospital in Chennai is granted a licence permitting it to store and administer essential narcotic drugs like morphine for palliative care patients, requiring maintenance of detailed registers and periodic inspection by narcotic officers.
what_it_covers: A licence to manufacture narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances issued to a pharmaceutical company or Central Government factory.
A licence to cultivate opium poppy granted to farmers in notified areas of Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, or Uttar Pradesh for a specific crop season.
A licence permitting a wholesaler or distributor to purchase and sell manufactured drugs or psychotropic substances within prescribed limits and conditions.
A licence authorising import or export of narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances for medical or scientific purposes.
A licence granted to a hospital, clinic, or research institution to possess and use essential narcotic drugs for legitimate medical or scientific purposes.
what_it_excludes: Unauthorised or forged permits purporting to allow dealings in narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances, which confer no legal protection under the Act.
An 'authorisation' issued under Section 9A or other specific provisions for controlled substances, which is a distinct instrument from a licence under the Act.

General business licences or trade licences issued under other laws (e.g., Shops and Establishments Act) that do not specifically authorise dealing in narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances under NDPS.
Activities conducted without any licence, even if the person believes in good faith that no licence is required, as such activities remain offences under Sections 8, 16, and 21.
A prescription issued by a registered medical practitioner permitting a patient to obtain narcotic drugs, which is not a 'licence' but a medical authorisation for personal therapeutic use.
definitions.why_it_matters: Possession of a valid licence is the critical legal distinction between a lawful activity and a punishable offence under the NDPS Act — operating without one triggers severe criminal liability under Sections 16, 21, and 26, including long terms of rigorous imprisonment. Conversely, a valid licence, complied with in accordance with its conditions, provides complete legal protection to the holder for activities that would otherwise be prohibited under Section 8.

definitions.definition: Licence fee means any fee payable to the Central Government or the State Government by a person holding or applying for a licence under the provisions of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, or any rule or order made thereunder, in consideration of the grant, renewal, or continuation of such licence authorising the cultivation, production, manufacture, possession, sale, purchase, transport, import, export, or use of narcotic drugs, psychotropic substances, or controlled substances.
definitions.plain_english: A licence fee is the money that a person or business must pay to the government in order to get or keep a legal permit to deal with narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances under this law. This could apply to a pharmaceutical company, a poppy farmer, or any other entity officially allowed to handle such controlled items. If you do not pay this fee, the government has strong powers to recover the money from you.
real_world_examples: A licensed pharmaceutical company in Hyderabad that manufactures codeine-based cough syrups pays an annual licence fee to the Central Government under the NDPS Act for its manufacturing licence; failure to pay allows the government to recover it as arrears of land revenue.

A government-approved opium cultivator in the Madhya Pradesh poppy belt pays a prescribed licence fee to the State Government for a cultivation licence each season under rules framed under the NDPS Act.

definitions.definition: A Magistrate under the NDPS Act refers to a Judicial Magistrate or Executive Magistrate as recognised under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, including a Metropolitan Magistrate or a Magistrate of the first class or second class specially empowered by the State Government, who is vested with jurisdiction to issue warrants, authorise detention, and perform other judicial functions prescribed under the Act.
definitions.plain_english: A Magistrate is a lower-level judicial officer who has the power to issue arrest warrants, order searches, and authorise the temporary detention of a person accused of a drug-related offence. Under the NDPS Act, different types of Magistrates have different levels of authority — for instance, a Judicial Magistrate can authorise custody for up to 15 days, while an Executive Magistrate can do so for only 7 days. They act as an important checkpoint in the criminal process before a case moves to a Special Court for trial.
real_world_examples: A Judicial Magistrate in Mumbai receives a forwarded accused who was arrested by the Narcotics Control Bureau for possession of heroin, and authorises police custody for 12 days under Section 167 of the CrPC as permitted under Section 36A of the NDPS Act.
A Metropolitan Magistrate in Delhi issues a search warrant under Section 41 of the NDPS Act allowing NCB officers to raid a suspected opium storage facility in Chandni Chowk.
A second class Magistrate specially empowered by the Rajasthan State Government issues an arrest warrant against a person reasonably suspected of trafficking cannabis across state borders.

An Executive Magistrate in a rural district of Punjab, upon receiving a forwarded accused from the local police, authorises detention for 7 days and later directs the accused to be forwarded to the designated Special Court as the offence involves a commercial quantity of heroin.

A Judicial Magistrate in Chennai, upon expiry of the initial detention period, determines that further detention is unnecessary and orders the accused to be forwarded to the Special Court having jurisdiction over NDPS offences in the area.
what_it_covers: A Judicial Magistrate (First Class or Metropolitan) empowered to authorise detention of an accused forwarded under Section 167 CrPC for up to 15 days in NDPS matters.
An Executive Magistrate specially empowered to authorise custody of an accused in NDPS cases for up to 7 days.
A Magistrate of the first or second class empowered by the State Government to issue search and arrest warrants under Section 41 of the NDPS Act.
A Magistrate who has the authority to forward an accused to the Special Court when the offence is triable by the Special Court under Section 36A.
what_it_excludes: A Special Court constituted under Section 36 of the NDPS Act, which is a distinct judicial forum with separate and broader trial jurisdiction over NDPS offences.
Gazetted officers or empowered officers of departments like NCB, customs, or police, who exercise executive powers of arrest and search but do not function as Magistrates.
Sessions Judges or High Court Judges, who belong to a higher tier of the judiciary and exercise appellate or bail jurisdiction distinct from the Magistrate's remand and warrant functions.
The Narcotics Commissioner or any administrative authority under the NDPS Act, who exercises regulatory and licensing functions but not judicial or magisterial powers.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification and empowerment of a Magistrate directly determines the permissible period of pre-trial detention (15 days for Judicial, 7 days for Executive) and the validity of arrest and search warrants issued under Section 41; any action taken by a person not falling within this definition would be without legal authority, rendering the detention, warrant, or search unlawful and potentially vitiating the entire prosecution. It also governs the procedural pathway for transferring accused persons to Special Courts, which is critical for cases involving commercial quantities or serious NDPS offences.

definitions.definition: 'Manufacture', in relation to narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances, includes— all processes other than production by which such drugs or substances may be obtained; refining of such drugs or substances; transformation of such drugs or substances; and making of preparation (otherwise than in a pharmacy on prescription) with or containing such drugs or substances.
definitions.plain_english: Manufacture means any process used to create, refine, convert, or prepare narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances, other than simply growing them. This includes turning raw materials into drugs, purifying impure drugs, chemically changing one drug into another, and mixing drugs into compounds or preparations outside of a licensed pharmacy acting on a doctor's prescription. Essentially, any human processing activity that results in a narcotic drug or psychotropic substance qualifies as manufacture.
real_world_examples: A clandestine laboratory in Himachal Pradesh converting morphine extracted from opium poppy into heroin through chemical acetylation — this is transformation of a narcotic drug and squarely falls under manufacture.

An illegal operation in Rajasthan refining raw opium (papaver somniferum latex) into medicinal-grade or street-grade opium concentrate by removing impurities — this constitutes refining of a narcotic drug under the definition.

A person in Mumbai mixing methamphetamine with cutting agents and binding them into tablet form without a pharmacy licence or doctor's prescription — this is making a preparation containing a psychotropic substance and amounts to manufacture.

A chemist in a Gujarat warehouse synthesising ephedrine from precursor controlled substances to produce pseudoephedrine-based stimulants outside any licensed facility — this involves a process other than production by which a psychotropic substance is obtained.

An unlicensed unit in Uttar Pradesh processing poppy straw concentrate into codeine-based cough syrups for illegal sale, without a pharmacist's prescription — this constitutes making of a preparation containing a narcotic drug outside a licensed pharmacy.

A group in Manipur transforming cannabis resin (charas) through solvent extraction into hashish oil (liquid hashish) for local distribution — this transformation of a cannabis derivative constitutes manufacture under the NDPS Act.
what_it_covers: All chemical or physical processes (other than cultivation/production) by which a narcotic drug or psychotropic substance is obtained, including synthesis from precursors.
Refining of impure or raw narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances to increase purity or potency, such as purifying raw opium into medicinal opium.
Transformation of one narcotic drug or psychotropic substance into another, such as converting morphine into heroin or codeine.
Making preparations containing narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances outside a licensed pharmacy acting on a valid prescription, such as tablet-pressing or syrup-mixing operations.
Any extraction process (other than direct cultivation harvest) by which a narcotic substance is isolated from plant or chemical material, such as extracting cocaine alkaloids from coca leaf.
what_it_excludes: Production — i.e., the direct agricultural or natural cultivation and harvesting of narcotic plants such as the opium poppy or cannabis plant — which is separately defined and governed under the Act.
Preparation of a drug by a licensed pharmacist in a registered pharmacy acting strictly on a valid doctor's prescription, which is explicitly carved out from the definition.
Mere possession, transport, or sale of a narcotic drug or psychotropic substance without any processing, refining, transforming, or compounding activity.
Cultivation of coca plants, cannabis plants, or opium poppies, which falls under 'production' or cultivation-specific provisions and not under manufacture.

Scientific or research activities conducted under a valid Central Government authorisation or licence that may involve handling but not independently manufacturing such substances for commercial or distribution purposes.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act constitutes 'manufacture' is critical because it attracts the stringent penal provisions under Sections 17 (manufactured drugs — lesser quantity), 18 (manufactured drugs — commercial quantity), and 22 (psychotropic substances) of the NDPS Act, which prescribe rigorous imprisonment ranging from 10 years to 20 years and heavy fines, with mandatory minimum sentences for commercial quantity. Establishing manufacture as opposed to mere possession or transport significantly escalates the severity of the charge and the applicable punishment.

definitions.definition: 'Manufactured drug' means all coca derivatives, medicinal cannabis, opium derivatives and poppy straw concentrate; and any other narcotic substance or preparation which the Central Government may, having regard to the available information as to its nature or to a decision, if any, under any International Convention, by notification in the Official Gazette, declare to be a manufactured drug; but does not include any narcotic substance or preparation which the Central Government may, having regard to the available information as to its nature or to a decision, if any, under any International Convention, by notification in the Official Gazette, declare not to be a manufactured drug.
definitions.plain_english: A 'manufactured drug' is a narcotic substance that has been processed or chemically derived from natural drug sources, such as cocaine products derived from coca leaves, medically used cannabis, derivatives of opium, or concentrated poppy straw. It also includes any other narcotic substance or preparation that the Central Government officially declares to be a manufactured drug through a gazette notification. Essentially, it covers drugs that are not in their raw natural form but have undergone some level of processing, refinement, or chemical transformation.
real_world_examples: A pharmaceutical company in Mumbai holding a government licence manufactures morphine tablets (an opium derivative) for use in hospitals — morphine being an opium derivative, it qualifies as a manufactured drug under the NDPS Act, and the company must comply with all licensing and record-keeping requirements.

A drug trafficking network in Delhi is found in possession of heroin, which is diacetylmorphine derived from opium — heroin is an opium derivative and therefore a manufactured drug, making the accused liable under Section 21 of the NDPS Act for possession of a manufactured drug.

Customs officers at Chennai port intercept a shipment containing cocaine hydrochloride, a coca derivative — since coca derivatives fall squarely within the definition of manufactured drug, the importers face prosecution under the NDPS Act for smuggling a manufactured drug into India.

A licensed Narcotics Commissioner-approved facility in Rajasthan processes poppy straw to extract poppy straw concentrate for pharmaceutical export — the concentrate is a manufactured drug, and any diversion or unlicensed handling triggers serious penal consequences under the Act.

The Central Government issues a gazette notification declaring a new synthetic opioid compound found circulating in street markets in Kolkata to be a manufactured drug, bringing it under the full regulatory and penal framework of the NDPS Act.

A hospital pharmacist in Hyderabad is found illegally dispensing pethidine (an opium derivative) without a valid prescription — pethidine being a manufactured drug, the pharmacist faces enhanced penalties under Section 21 for unauthorised possession and supply of a manufactured drug.
what_it_covers: All coca derivatives including crude cocaine, ecgonine and its derivatives, cocaine (methyl ester of benzoyl-ecgonine and its salts), and preparations containing more than 0.1% cocaine.
Medicinal cannabis, being cannabis preparations used for medical or scientific purposes as recognised under the Act.
All opium derivatives including morphine, heroin (diacetylmorphine), codeine, pethidine, medicinal opium, and prepared opium.
Poppy straw concentrate, being the material arising when poppy straw has entered into a process for the concentration of its alkaloids.

Any other narcotic substance or preparation that the Central Government, by official gazette notification, expressly declares to be a manufactured drug based on its nature or international convention obligations.
what_it_excludes: Raw opium in its natural unprocessed form — opium as harvested from the opium poppy is separately defined and classified under 'opium', not as a manufactured drug.
Cannabis plant, ganja, and charas in their natural unprocessed states — these fall under the definition of 'cannabis (hemp)' and are regulated separately from manufactured drugs.
Coca leaves in their natural form, except where all ecgonine and cocaine alkaloids have been removed, which are separately defined and not classified as manufactured drugs.
Preparations containing not more than 0.1% cocaine, which are explicitly excluded from the definition of 'coca derivative' and therefore fall outside the scope of manufactured drugs.

Any narcotic substance or preparation that the Central Government, by official gazette notification, specifically declares not to be a manufactured drug, regardless of its chemical origin or derivation.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a substance qualifies as a 'manufactured drug' directly determines the applicable penal provision — possession, sale, purchase, transport, or use of a manufactured drug attracts punishment under Section 21 of the NDPS Act, which prescribes rigorous imprisonment of up to twenty years and heavy fines depending on the quantity involved. Correct classification as a manufactured drug also triggers mandatory licensing, record-keeping, import-export controls, and the enhanced scrutiny and forfeiture provisions applicable specifically to narcotic drugs under the Act.

definitions.definition: "Medicinal cannabis" is not separately and formally defined in the Act, but it forms a constituent part of the definition of "manufactured drug" under Section 2, which includes "all coca derivatives, medicinal cannabis, opium derivatives and poppy straw concentrate." In legislative and regulatory practice, medicinal cannabis refers to cannabis or cannabis-derived preparations that have been processed or prepared for therapeutic, medical, or scientific use, as distinct from raw cannabis plant material (ganja or charas).
definitions.plain_english: Medicinal cannabis refers to cannabis that has been specially prepared or processed for use as a medicine or in scientific research. It is different from raw cannabis products like ganja or charas, which are used as intoxicants. Because it is classified as a 'manufactured drug' under the NDPS Act, it is subject to strict rules about who can produce, store, sell, or use it — essentially only those with proper government licences or authorisations for medical and scientific purposes.
real_world_examples: A government-licensed pharmaceutical company in Uttarakhand obtains a licence to process cannabis plant extracts into standardised tinctures or capsules intended for pain management research — such preparations would qualify as medicinal cannabis under the Act.

A Central Government factory in India is authorised to manufacture cannabis-based medicines for supply to government hospitals for use in treating conditions like epilepsy or chronic pain, making the product a regulated medicinal cannabis item under NDPS.

A state government issues a permit to a research institution in Mumbai to possess and use cannabis extracts in controlled clinical trials for neurological disorders — the extracted and prepared cannabis compound used in the trial falls within the ambit of medicinal cannabis.

An importer applies to the Narcotics Commissioner for authorisation to import a cannabis-derived pharmaceutical (such as a CBD-based medicine approved abroad) for compassionate use in Indian hospitals — the imported preparation is treated as a manufactured drug (medicinal cannabis) requiring strict compliance with NDPS licensing norms.

A wholesale drug dealer is found in possession of processed cannabis tinctures without a valid NDPS licence — the prosecution charges him under provisions governing manufactured drugs, specifically invoking the medicinal cannabis classification to establish the offence.
what_it_covers: Cannabis plant extracts or tinctures prepared and standardised for therapeutic or medicinal purposes by licensed manufacturers.
Cannabis-derived pharmaceutical preparations (such as oils, capsules, or solutions) manufactured under government authorisation for medical or scientific use.
Processed cannabis concentrates or formulations supplied by Central Government factories for use in hospitals or research institutions.
Cannabis-based medicines imported under special NDPS authorisation for compassionate or clinical trial use within India.
what_it_excludes: Raw ganja (flowering or fruiting tops of the cannabis plant not accompanied by further processing), which is separately defined under 'cannabis (hemp)' and not classified as medicinal cannabis.
Charas (separated resin of the cannabis plant in crude or purified form), which falls under the 'cannabis (hemp)' definition and is not treated as medicinal cannabis.
The cannabis plant itself in its natural, uncultivated state, which is covered by the definition of 'cannabis plant' rather than medicinal cannabis.
Cannabis seeds and leaves when not accompanied by flowering tops and not subjected to any manufacturing process, as these do not meet the processed/prepared threshold for medicinal cannabis.
Any preparation or product that the Central Government has notified as not being a manufactured drug, thereby removing it from the medicinal cannabis classification.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of a substance as medicinal cannabis determines that it is a 'manufactured drug' under Section 2 of the NDPS Act, triggering the full range of stringent licensing, possession, sale, transport, and import/export obligations applicable to manufactured drugs, and exposing any unlicensed dealing to serious penal consequences including rigorous imprisonment. Conversely, only substances meeting this classification can be lawfully produced, held, or supplied for medical or scientific purposes under a valid NDPS licence or authorisation, distinguishing them from illicit cannabis forms.

definitions.definition: "Medicinal opium" means opium which has been subjected to processes to adapt it for medicinal use in accordance with the requirements of the Indian Pharmacopoeia or any other pharmacopoeia notified by the Central Government, whether in powder form or mixed with neutral materials, and is a component of 'manufactured drug' under this Act.
definitions.plain_english: Medicinal opium is opium that has been specially processed and purified to meet pharmaceutical standards so it can be used as a medicine. It is different from raw opium because it has undergone specific chemical or physical treatment to make it safe and suitable for medical purposes. In India, it is tightly controlled and can only be produced, sold, or used under strict government licences.
real_world_examples: A Central Government factory in Ghaziabad processes raw opium harvested from licensed poppy cultivators in Madhya Pradesh into medicinal opium powder conforming to Indian Pharmacopoeia standards, which is then supplied to licensed pharmaceutical companies for further manufacture of painkillers.

A licensed pharmaceutical company in Maharashtra obtains a consignment of medicinal opium from the Government Opium and Alkaloid Works, Neemuch, to manufacture morphine tablets prescribed for palliative care patients in government hospitals.

A licensed wholesale dealer in Delhi applies for a permit under the NDPS Act and relevant state rules to store and distribute medicinal opium to licensed retailers and hospitals, ensuring the supply chain remains within the legally authorised framework.

A customs officer at Chennai port intercepts an unlabelled shipment of processed opium powder. Forensic analysis confirms it meets the pharmacopoeial specification for medicinal opium, and the importer is found to lack the required import authorisation under the NDPS Act, triggering prosecution for illegal import of a manufactured drug.

A government-authorised Ayurvedic pharmaceutical unit in Uttarakhand uses medicinal opium as an ingredient in a compound preparation (e.g., Dover's Powder equivalent) under a valid licence, maintaining the mandatory quantity registers prescribed by the Narcotics Commissioner.
what_it_covers: Opium that has been subjected to pharmacopoeial processes (e.g., drying, powdering, standardisation of morphine content) as specified in the Indian Pharmacopoeia or a notified pharmacopoeia.
Powdered or granulated opium mixed with neutral or inert materials (such as lactose) to achieve a standardised medicinal grade suitable for pharmaceutical formulation.

Medicinal opium produced in Central Government factories (e.g., Government Opium and Alkaloid Works, Ghaziabad or Neemuch) and supplied through authorised channels for medical and scientific purposes.
Any preparation falling within the definition of 'manufactured drug' by virtue of containing medicinal opium as a constituent ingredient.
what_it_excludes: Raw or crude opium (the coagulated juice of the opium poppy) that has not been subjected to pharmacopoeial processing, which is governed separately as 'opium' under the Act.
Prepared opium (opium prepared for smoking), which is a distinct category under the NDPS Act and is defined and regulated separately.
Opium derivatives such as morphine, codeine, heroin, or thebaine, which are classified as 'opium derivatives' and not as medicinal opium, even though they are derived from the same source.
Poppy straw concentrate and other manufactured drugs that are derived from the opium poppy but fall under different sub-categories of 'manufactured drug'.
Illicitly processed opium that has not been produced in accordance with pharmacopoeial standards or under a valid government authorisation, which would be treated as contraband opium.
definitions.why_it_matters: Because medicinal opium is classified as a 'manufactured drug' under Section 2 of the NDPS Act, any production, possession, sale, purchase, transport, import, or export without a valid licence or authorisation constitutes a serious cognizable offence attracting rigorous imprisonment and heavy fines under Sections 15–19 and related provisions; conversely, when properly licensed, it may lawfully be used for medical and scientific purposes under Section 9, exempting authorised persons from those penal provisions.

definitions.definition: The term 'minor' is not formally defined in the NDPS Act, but as used in Section 32B, it refers to a person who has not attained the age of majority under Indian law, i.e., a person below eighteen years of age as per the Indian Majority Act, 1875. The involvement of such persons — whether as victims affected by a narcotic or psychotropic substance offence, or as instruments used by an offender to commit such offence — constitutes an aggravating factor warranting imposition of punishment higher than the prescribed minimum.
definitions.plain_english: A 'minor' under the NDPS Act refers to a child or young person below 18 years of age. The law treats the involvement of minors in drug-related offences very seriously — either when children are harmed by drugs or when adults use children to carry out drug crimes. If a minor is involved in any of these ways, the court can give the accused a heavier punishment than the usual minimum.
real_world_examples: A drug peddler in Mumbai recruits a 14-year-old street child to deliver small packets of heroin to customers, thereby using a minor for the commission of a drug offence under the NDPS Act, triggering enhanced punishment under Section 32B.

In Delhi, a school canteen operator near a government secondary school is found supplying cannabis-laced edibles to students aged 13–17 years, making the minors 'affected' by the offence and exposing the operator to higher-than-minimum sentencing.

A drug trafficking gang in Punjab is discovered using children between the ages of 10 and 16 as couriers to transport ganja across village boundaries, exploiting their age to avoid detection — a clear case of minors being used for commission of an NDPS offence.

In Chennai, a man is convicted under the NDPS Act for operating a drug distribution network near a school that has resulted in addiction among several students under 18; the court invokes Section 32B noting that minors were affected, thereby imposing a sentence beyond the statutory minimum.

A drug supplier in Kolkata is found selling synthetic psychotropic substances directly to college students aged 16–17 at a coaching centre; the court considers both the proximity to an educational institution and the fact that minors were affected while determining enhanced sentencing.
what_it_covers: A person below 18 years of age who is directly harmed or adversely affected by a narcotic or psychotropic substance offence, such as a child who becomes addicted due to the offender's activities.
A child or adolescent who is recruited, coerced, or used by an adult offender as a tool or agent for committing an NDPS offence, such as acting as a drug carrier or delivery person.
School-going children or students under 18 who are targeted by drug sellers operating near educational institutions, thereby falling within the class of 'minors affected' by the offence.
Any person under the age of majority (18 years) who, without being a principal offender, becomes involved in the chain of a drug offence at the instigation or direction of an adult accused.
what_it_excludes: Persons who have attained the age of 18 years and are therefore adults under Indian law, even if they appear youthful or are students.

A minor who independently and voluntarily commits an NDPS offence without being used or directed by an adult offender — in such cases the minor may be dealt with under juvenile justice law, but the adult aggravating factor under Section 32B does not apply to the minor themselves.
Situations where a minor is merely present at the scene of a drug offence but is neither affected by the substance nor actively used for the commission of the offence.
Adults who claim minority falsely — Section 32B applies only where the person is genuinely below 18 years of age as established by evidence before the court.
definitions.why_it_matters: The involvement of a minor — either as a person affected by an NDPS offence or as someone used to commit it — is a statutory aggravating factor under Section 32B that empowers the court to impose punishment exceeding the prescribed minimum term of imprisonment or fine. This directly raises the sentencing exposure of the accused and signals a legislative policy of heightened protection for children in the context of narcotic and psychotropic substance offences.

definitions.definition: As used in Section 35 of the NDPS Act, 'motive' is a component of 'culpable mental state' and refers to the underlying reason, purpose, or drive that impels a person to commit an act constituting an offence under the Act. The court shall presume the existence of such motive in any prosecution requiring a culpable mental state, and it is for the accused to rebut this presumption by proving on the balance of probabilities beyond reasonable doubt that no such mental state existed.
definitions.plain_english: Motive means the reason or personal purpose behind why someone does something illegal under the drug law. For example, a person might sell drugs because they need money, or smuggle narcotics because they were promised a large payment. Under this law, the court assumes a person had a motive for committing the drug offence, and the burden falls on the accused to prove they did not.
real_world_examples: A drug peddler in Mumbai is arrested carrying one kilogram of heroin. The prosecution argues his motive was financial gain from selling the drug. The court presumes this motive existed, and the accused must show he had no such purpose — for instance, he was unknowingly carrying the packet for someone else.

A pharmacy owner in Delhi is charged with supplying controlled psychotropic substances without a licence. The court presumes his motive was to profit illegally. The accused attempts to rebut this by showing he believed he was dispensing under a valid prescription.

A carrier caught at Chennai airport with cocaine hidden in his baggage claims he was unaware of its contents. The prosecution establishes motive as financial reward promised by a drug syndicate. The court presumes the motive, and the accused must prove he had no knowledge or reason to act as a drug courier.

A farmer in Rajasthan is prosecuted for illegally cultivating opium poppy beyond the licensed area. The prosecution argues his motive was to earn extra income from illicit opium trade. Under Section 35, the court presumes this motive and the farmer must demonstrate absence of any culpable mental state.

A teenager in Bengaluru is prosecuted for possessing cannabis beyond the small quantity threshold. Investigators allege his motive was to supply to fellow students for profit. The presumption of motive under Section 35 shifts the burden onto the accused to disprove any commercial intent.
semantic_tags: financial or personal drive to offend
what_it_covers: Financial gain as a reason for trafficking, selling, or smuggling narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances.
Personal addiction-driven purpose where an accused acquires or possesses drugs to feed their own dependency.
Ideological, coercive, or social reasons such as acting under threat, peer pressure, or to settle debts by delivering narcotics for a syndicate.
Commercial motives of a manufacturer or supplier who produces illicit drugs for profit without a licence.
Revenge or retaliation as a reason to introduce drugs into a rival's premises to implicate them — prosecution can allege such motive under Section 35.
what_it_excludes: Purely accidental possession where there is no underlying purpose or reason whatsoever — if the accused successfully rebuts the presumption with credible evidence of innocent handling.

Motive as a standalone element required to be independently proven by the prosecution — Section 35 presumes it exists and places the burden on the accused, so prosecution need not separately establish it.
Lawful and licensed activities performed under authorisation, where the purpose is regulated and the question of culpable motive does not arise under the Act.

Situations where the act itself does not require a culpable mental state as a statutory ingredient — motive as part of culpable mental state is only relevant where the offence provision expressly or impliedly requires mental element.
definitions.why_it_matters: The inclusion of motive as part of 'culpable mental state' under Section 35 creates a statutory presumption against the accused in NDPS prosecutions, effectively reversing the ordinary burden of proof and compelling the accused to disprove their mental state. This presumption can be decisive in securing convictions for drug trafficking, possession, and related offences, as courts do not require independent prosecution evidence of motive once the act is established.

definitions.plain_english: A narcotic drug refers to a specific set of naturally derived and chemically processed substances that are strictly controlled by Indian law because of their potential for abuse, addiction, and harm. This includes substances like opium, cannabis, coca leaf, poppy straw, and all drugs manufactured or derived from these. Possession, sale, or trafficking of any of these without proper authorisation is a serious criminal offence in India.
real_world_examples: A courier intercepted at Indira Gandhi International Airport, New Delhi, carrying concealed packets of heroin (an opium derivative) in a false-bottomed suitcase — heroin qualifies as a narcotic drug under NDPS as a manufactured drug (opium derivative).
A farmer in Malwa, Punjab, found cultivating opium poppy beyond the licensed area and selling raw opium to unauthorised buyers — opium is explicitly listed as a narcotic drug under the Act.

A raid by the Narcotics Control Bureau in Himachal Pradesh seizing large quantities of charas (cannabis resin) extracted from wild cannabis plants growing in Kullu valley — charas falls within the definition of cannabis (hemp), which is a narcotic drug.

A pharmaceutical company in Mumbai found diverting poppy straw concentrate, licensed for medicinal use, into the illegal market — poppy straw concentrate is a manufactured drug and thus a narcotic drug under NDPS.
Police in Goa arresting a foreign national found in possession of cocaine at a beach party — cocaine is a coca derivative and a manufactured drug, squarely within the definition of narcotic drug.

A small-quantity case in Kerala where a person is found consuming brown sugar (diacetylmorphine), an opium derivative, triggering Section 27 of NDPS dealing with personal consumption of narcotic drugs.
what_it_covers: Coca leaf and all coca derivatives including cocaine and ecgonine salts
Cannabis (hemp) in all its forms including charas, ganja and cannabis-based preparations
Opium in raw, prepared and medicinal forms, including opium derivatives such as heroin and morphine
Poppy straw and poppy straw concentrate extracted from the opium poppy plant
Any other narcotic substance or preparation notified as a manufactured drug by the Central Government via Official Gazette
Medicinal cannabis when diverted or used outside the scope of a valid licence or authorisation
what_it_excludes: Psychotropic substances such as amphetamines, LSD or benzodiazepines — these are separately defined and governed under the psychotropic substance definition in Section 2
Controlled substances (precursor chemicals) used in manufacture of narcotic drugs — these are separately defined as 'controlled substance' and carry distinct obligations
Coca leaf from which all ecgonine, cocaine and other ecgonine alkaloids have been fully removed — expressly excluded from the definition of coca leaf and hence not a narcotic drug
Preparations containing not more than 0.1 per cent of cocaine — explicitly excluded from the coca leaf and coca derivative definitions
Seeds and leaves of the cannabis plant when not accompanied by the flowering or fruiting tops — excluded from the definition of ganja and thus not per se a narcotic drug
Flavouring agents derived from poppy seeds used in food, where no narcotic alkaloid is present — falls outside the operative scope of narcotic drug provisions
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a substance qualifies as a 'narcotic drug' is the threshold determination for nearly every penal provision under NDPS — including Sections 8 (prohibition), 27 (personal consumption), 23 (import/export), and 31A (death penalty for repeat trafficking offences) — and determines whether mandatory minimum sentences, commercial or small quantity thresholds, and preventive detention provisions are triggered or remain inapplicable.

definitions.definition: 'Narcotic drug' means coca leaf, cannabis (hemp), opium, poppy straw and includes all manufactured drugs and such other substances, whether natural or synthetic, as the Central Government may, having regard to the available information as to their nature or to a decision, if any, under any International Convention, by notification in the Official Gazette, declare to be narcotic drugs.
definitions.plain_english: Narcotic drugs are a specific category of substances that are controlled under Indian law because of their potential for abuse and addiction. This category includes well-known substances like opium, cannabis (ganja, charas), coca leaf, poppy straw, and all products manufactured from them. The Central Government can also add new substances to this list by issuing a notification if they are found to be similar in nature or are covered under an international treaty signed by India.
real_world_examples: A courier intercepted at Indira Gandhi International Airport, New Delhi carrying concealed pouches of heroin (an opium derivative) inside luggage — heroin qualifies as a narcotic drug under NDPS as a manufactured drug (opium derivative), triggering prosecution under Section 21.

Punjab Police seizing large quantities of poppy husk (doda/phukki) from a truck near Amritsar — poppy straw is explicitly listed as a narcotic drug, making possession and transportation punishable under Sections 15 and 29.

Bengaluru Narcotics Control Bureau busting a hashish oil (liquid hashish/charas) manufacturing unit — cannabis and its concentrated resin preparations are narcotic drugs, attracting rigorous imprisonment under Section 20.

Maharashtra ATS arresting a smuggler carrying blocks of compressed ganja from Andhra Pradesh destined for Mumbai — ganja, as a form of cannabis hemp, is a narcotic drug and inter-state transport without authorisation is an offence under Section 9 read with Section 20.

Customs officers at Chennai Port seizing a shipment misdeclared as herbal tea but found to contain cocaine (a coca derivative) — cocaine falls within narcotic drugs as a manufactured drug, making import into India punishable under Section 27B and Section 29.

Rajasthan Police arresting a farmer for illicit cultivation of opium poppy beyond the licensed acreage, with raw opium extracted and stored — opium is a narcotic drug and unlicensed production and possession attract Section 18 of the NDPS Act.
what_it_covers: Coca leaf and all coca derivatives including cocaine, ecgonine and their salts and preparations containing more than 0.1% cocaine
Cannabis (hemp) in all its forms including charas, ganja, hashish oil, and any mixture or drink prepared therefrom
Opium including raw opium, medicinal opium, prepared opium and opium derivatives such as heroin, morphine and codeine
Poppy straw and poppy straw concentrate obtained from the opium poppy plant

Any additional substance declared by the Central Government by notification in the Official Gazette to be a narcotic drug based on international convention decisions or available scientific information
what_it_excludes: Psychotropic substances (such as amphetamines, LSD, or benzodiazepines) which are regulated separately under the NDPS Act as a distinct category
Controlled substances (precursor chemicals used in manufacture of narcotic drugs) which have their own separate definition and regulatory regime under Section 2
Coca leaf preparations containing not more than 0.1 per cent of cocaine, which are excluded from the definition of coca leaf and consequently from the narcotic drugs category
Seeds and leaves of the cannabis plant when not accompanied by the flowering or fruiting tops, which are excluded from the definition of ganja/cannabis hemp
Industrial hemp or other botanical uses of cannabis plant parts not meeting the definitional threshold under cannabis (hemp) as defined in Section 2
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a substance qualifies as a 'narcotic drug' determines the applicability of the entire punitive and regulatory framework under the NDPS Act, including offences relating to production, manufacture, possession, sale, transport, import, export and financing under Sections 4, 9, 15–27B, 29, 44, and 64A. The classification directly governs whether small quantity or commercial quantity thresholds apply, which in turn determines the severity of punishment — including whether mandatory minimum sentences or the death penalty provisions are attracted.

definitions.definition: "Narcotics Commissioner" means the Narcotics Commissioner appointed by the Central Government under section 5 of this Act, who is vested with powers and functions as prescribed, including the superintendence of the cultivation of the opium poppy and the production of opium, and such other functions as may be assigned under this Act.
definitions.plain_english: The Narcotics Commissioner is a senior government official appointed by the Central Government to oversee and regulate the legal cultivation of opium poppy and production of opium in India. This officer acts as the chief administrative authority under the NDPS Act for managing licit narcotic-related activities. The Commissioner also exercises supervisory and regulatory powers over officers and operations related to narcotics control as assigned by the Central Government.
real_world_examples: The Narcotics Commissioner, headquartered in Gwalior (Madhya Pradesh), issues licences to farmers in Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan permitting them to legally cultivate opium poppy under strictly monitored conditions each season.

When a farmer in Neemuch, Madhya Pradesh, is found to have cultivated opium poppy beyond the licensed area, the Narcotics Commissioner's office initiates action for excess cultivation and initiates confiscation proceedings under the NDPS Act.

The Narcotics Commissioner coordinates with the Central Bureau of Narcotics to verify and certify the quantity of opium produced by licensed cultivators before it is handed over to government factories for processing into medicinal opium or opium derivatives.

Under Section 75, during an inquiry or investigation into alleged diversion of licit opium, officers of the Narcotics Commissioner's establishment are empowered to enter licensed premises, inspect records, and seize documents as part of the supervisory function.

The Narcotics Commissioner issues policy circulars setting the minimum qualifying yield (MQY) for opium farmers, and farmers who fail to meet this yield threshold are denied renewal of their cultivation licences for the following season.
what_it_covers: A Central Government-appointed officer designated as 'Narcotics Commissioner' under Section 5 of the NDPS Act with statutory powers over licit opium cultivation and production.
The officer responsible for superintending the licensing of opium poppy cultivation by farmers in designated states such as Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, and Uttar Pradesh.
An authority empowered under Section 75 to enter, inspect, and investigate premises, records, and operations connected with narcotics for regulatory and enforcement purposes.
The officer who oversees the collection, weighment, and delivery of opium produced by licensed cultivators to Central Government factories.
The Commissioner's subordinate officers and establishment who act under the Commissioner's delegated authority in performing day-to-day regulatory functions.
what_it_excludes: State-level narcotics officers or state government officials who exercise powers under state excise or drug laws but are not appointed as Narcotics Commissioner under the NDPS Act.

Officers of the Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB), which is a separate authority under Section 4 of the NDPS Act concerned primarily with enforcement and counter-narcotics operations rather than licit cultivation oversight.
Private individuals, licensed dealers, or pharmaceutical company representatives involved in the narcotics supply chain, none of whom hold the statutory office of Narcotics Commissioner.
Customs or police officers who may exercise NDPS powers under Sections 41–53 but are not appointed to the specific post of Narcotics Commissioner.
Officers appointed under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 who regulate medicinal drug manufacture but do not derive authority from the NDPS Act's Narcotics Commissioner provisions.
definitions.why_it_matters: The identity of the Narcotics Commissioner is legally significant because only this officer (or those duly authorised by this officer) can lawfully superintend and licence opium poppy cultivation under the NDPS Act; any cultivation undertaken without such authorisation constitutes an offence under Section 18. Actions taken under Sections 5 and 75—including inspections, seizures, and licence cancellations—derive their validity from the lawful exercise of the Narcotics Commissioner's statutory authority, and unauthorised exercise of these powers can vitiate proceedings.

definitions.definition: The Narcotics Control Bureau is the central law enforcement and intelligence agency constituted under sub-section (3) of section 4 of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, headed by a Director General, and empowered to coordinate drug law enforcement activities, undertake controlled delivery operations, and assist in proceedings related to illegally acquired property under the Act.
definitions.plain_english: The Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB) is India's top central government agency responsible for fighting drug trafficking and enforcing laws related to narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances. It is led by a Director General and works alongside police, customs, and other agencies to investigate drug-related crimes. The NCB can conduct special operations like 'controlled deliveries' where drug shipments are allowed to proceed under surveillance to catch bigger criminal networks.
real_world_examples: The NCB conducted a controlled delivery operation at Mumbai Port, allowing a consignment of heroin concealed in cargo to be tracked to its intended recipient, leading to the arrest of a major drug trafficking syndicate in 2021.

The NCB coordinated with the DEA (USA) and Afghan authorities to track an international drug consignment destined for Delhi, using the controlled delivery mechanism under Section 50A to dismantle a cross-border narcotics network.

NCB officers in Chennai assisted the Administrator appointed under Section 68G in identifying and freezing illegally acquired properties of a drug financier, providing financial intelligence and operational support during the proceedings.

The NCB's Bengaluru zonal unit assisted the Appellate Tribunal under Section 68T by furnishing investigation records and surveillance data in a case involving proceeds of drug trafficking disguised as legitimate real estate investments.

During the Aryan Khan cruise ship case in 2021, NCB officers exercised their powers under the NDPS Act to investigate alleged possession and consumption of narcotic drugs aboard a vessel in Mumbai waters.

The NCB coordinated with the Narcotics Department of Himachal Pradesh to intercept a large cannabis consignment being transported from Kullu to Delhi, with NCB officers taking custody of the accused for further investigation under the NDPS Act.
what_it_covers: The Director General of the NCB and all officers of the NCB authorised to conduct investigations, searches, seizures, and arrests under the NDPS Act.
Controlled delivery operations both within India and to foreign countries, undertaken by the NCB or officers authorised by the Director General under Section 50A.

Assistance provided by NCB officers to the Administrator, competent authority, and Appellate Tribunal in proceedings related to forfeiture and recovery of illegally acquired property under Chapter VA.
Coordination with foreign law enforcement agencies and competent authorities of foreign countries for cross-border controlled delivery of drug consignments.
Intelligence gathering, surveillance, and enforcement activities targeting illicit trafficking of narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances across India.
what_it_excludes: State Narcotics Departments and state police narcotics cells, which are separate agencies not constituted under the NCB and operate under state government authority.

The Central Bureau of Narcotics (CBN) under the Ministry of Finance, which is a distinct body responsible for licensing, cultivation control, and international treaty obligations — separate from the NCB.
Customs and Central Excise officers, who are listed separately under Section 68T and are not part of the Narcotics Control Bureau even when assisting in NDPS proceedings.
Private individuals, informants, or non-gazetted government employees who may assist NCB operations but do not constitute members or officers of the Bureau.
The Narcotics Commissioner, who is a separate authority under the NDPS Act distinct from the NCB and its Director General.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a law enforcement action is taken by the NCB or its authorised officers directly determines the legality and jurisdiction of operations like controlled delivery under Section 50A — actions taken without NCB authorisation would be invalid and could render arrests, seizures, and prosecutions liable to challenge. NCB officer status also triggers mandatory obligations on other agencies such as Customs, Income Tax, and police to assist in proceedings under Section 68T.

definitions.definition: A 'notified officer' means an officer notified under section 53 of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, who is empowered to exercise the powers of arrest, search, and seizure under the Act, and who is specifically designated by the Central Government or a State Government by notification in the Official Gazette for such purposes.
definitions.plain_english: A notified officer is a government official who has been officially designated and published in a government gazette to carry out drug-related arrests and seizures under India's anti-narcotics law. Think of them as specially authorised officers — not just any police officer, but one specifically named or empowered by the government to act under the NDPS Act. They have special legal powers to arrest people and seize drugs or related property, and must report any illegally acquired property of an arrested person to the competent authority within 90 days.
real_world_examples: A Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB) officer notified under Section 53 raids a warehouse in Mumbai, arrests a drug trafficker, and seizes large quantities of heroin and cash; under Section 57A, the officer must report the trafficker's illegally acquired properties — such as benami land, luxury vehicles, and bank accounts — to the competent authority within 90 days.

A Customs officer notified under Section 53 apprehends a person at Chennai airport attempting to smuggle methamphetamine; upon invoking Chapter VA, the officer files a report of the arrested person's illegally acquired assets, including real estate holdings, within the statutory 90-day period.

A Narcotics Control Bureau officer in Delhi arrests a known drug financier; being a notified officer, the officer is obligated under Section 57A to identify and report all properties suspected to be illegally acquired by the financier to the jurisdictional competent authority before the 90-day deadline.

A Revenue Intelligence officer notified under Section 53 seizes a large consignment of opium in Rajasthan and arrests the carrier; the notified officer subsequently traces bank deposits and agricultural land registered in the name of the carrier's relatives and reports them as illegally acquired properties within 90 days as mandated by Section 57A.

A State excise officer, duly notified under Section 53 in a gazette notification issued by the State Government of Maharashtra, arrests a local drug distributor; the officer then compiles a report of the distributor's two commercial properties and three vehicles suspected to have been purchased from drug proceeds and submits it to the competent authority within the prescribed timeframe.
what_it_covers: Officers of the Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB) who have been notified by the Central Government under Section 53 to exercise powers of arrest and seizure under the NDPS Act.
Customs officers, Revenue Intelligence officers, and Border Security Force officers who are officially designated by gazette notification under Section 53 and empowered to act under the NDPS Act.

State excise officers or police officers notified by the respective State Government under Section 53, who carry out arrests or seizures of narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances within their jurisdiction.
Any gazetted officer from a department recognised under Section 53 who has been specifically empowered by a notification in the Official Gazette to perform enforcement functions under the NDPS Act.
what_it_excludes: Ordinary police officers who have not been specifically notified under Section 53, even if they are otherwise empowered to make arrests under the Code of Criminal Procedure.
Private individuals or informants who may assist in drug-related investigations but hold no official gazette-notified status under Section 53 of the NDPS Act.
Judicial officers, magistrates, or court officials who may be involved in NDPS proceedings but are not empowered to make arrests or seizures under Section 53.
Officers whose notifications under Section 53 have been revoked or who belong to departments not recognised under Section 53, regardless of their seniority or rank.

definitions.definition: An 'occupier' is a person who occupies or is in actual possession and control of any house, room, enclosure, space, place, animal, or conveyance, and who, if such person knowingly permits such premises or property to be used by another person for the commission of an offence under the Act, shall be liable to punishment under Section 25.
definitions.plain_english: An occupier is someone who is actually using, living in, or in charge of a place or property — such as a rented flat, shop, warehouse, or vehicle — even if they do not legally own it. If such a person knowingly allows someone else to use that place or property to commit a drug-related crime, they can be punished just as severely as the person who actually committed the offence. The key idea is actual control or possession, not legal ownership.
real_world_examples: A tenant renting a flat in Mumbai who knowingly allows drug peddlers to store or sell narcotics from the flat can be prosecuted as an occupier under Section 25, even though the landlord owns the property.
A warehouse manager in Delhi who has control over a godown and permits it to be used by traffickers to conceal large quantities of heroin can be held liable as an occupier under the NDPS Act.

A truck driver in Rajasthan who has physical control of a commercial vehicle and knowingly allows contraband cannabis to be loaded and transported in it can be prosecuted as the occupier of the conveyance.

A shopkeeper in Kolkata who occupies a commercial space and permits a portion of the backroom to be used by associates for manufacturing synthetic drugs can be punished as the occupier under Section 25.

A hotel manager in Goa who knowingly allows specific rooms to be repeatedly used by guests for consumption and sale of psychotropic substances can be treated as the occupier of those premises and held criminally liable.
A stable owner in Punjab who has control over an enclosure and knowingly allows it to be used for concealing poppy straw can be prosecuted as the occupier of that space.
what_it_covers: A tenant or lessee who has actual possession and use of a residential or commercial property and knowingly permits drug-related activities on those premises.
A person in charge of or operating a vehicle, vessel, or aircraft (conveyance) who knowingly allows it to be used for transporting or concealing narcotics or psychotropic substances.

A manager, caretaker, or any individual exercising de facto control over a warehouse, enclosure, or open space who knowingly permits it to be used for manufacture, storage, or sale of controlled substances.
A person who shares occupation of a premises with an owner and knowingly facilitates drug offences by allowing access or use of that space to a third party.
An individual who has temporary but exclusive control of a place or conveyance (such as a chartered vehicle operator) and knowingly allows its use for committing an NDPS offence.
what_it_excludes: A property owner who has leased or rented out the premises and has no actual control, possession, or knowledge of the illegal activities being carried out by the occupier or tenant.
A person who occupies a premises but has no knowledge whatsoever that it is being used by another person for committing an NDPS offence — lack of knowledge negates liability under Section 25.
A person who merely visits or temporarily enters a premises but has no control, possession, or right to regulate its use cannot be treated as an occupier.
A co-resident or family member who lives on the premises but exercises no independent control or authority over it and is unaware of any drug-related activity.
An employee such as a domestic worker or security guard who occupies a post at the premises in a subordinate capacity but has no authority to permit or refuse use of the property.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as an 'occupier' under Section 25 determines whether they can be held criminally liable — with the same punishment as the principal offender — for knowingly permitting their premises or property to be used for an NDPS offence; establishing occupier status is therefore critical to prosecution, as it creates direct penal accountability for enabling drug crimes without personally committing them.
