definitions.definition: For the purposes of section 68F, 'transfer of property' means any disposition, conveyance, assignment, settlement, delivery, payment or other alienation of property and, without limiting the generality of the foregoing, includes: the creation of a trust in property; the grant or creation of any lease, mortgage, charge, easement, licence, power, partnership or interest in property; the exercise of a power of appointment of property vested in any person, not the owner of the property, to determine its disposition in favour of any person other than the donee of the power; and any transaction entered into by any person with intent thereby to diminish directly or indirectly the value of his own property and to increase the value of the property of any other person.
definitions.plain_english: A 'transfer of property' under this law means any way in which ownership, control, or benefit of a property is moved from one person to another. This includes selling, gifting, leasing, mortgaging, creating a trust, forming a partnership over the property, or any financial arrangement that shifts the property's value to someone else. Even transactions designed to reduce the value of a person's own property so that someone else benefits are treated as a transfer.
real_world_examples: A drug trafficker in Mumbai, facing investigation under NDPS Chapter VA, sells his flat in Andheri to a relative for a fraction of its market value to move it out of his name before forfeiture proceedings begin — this sale constitutes a 'transfer of property'.

An accused person in Delhi, whose properties are under inquiry, creates a trust naming his wife as trustee and transfers his farmland in Haryana into the trust to shield it from seizure — the creation of such a trust is explicitly covered as a transfer of property.

A narcotics offender in Chennai mortgages his commercial property to a private financier to raise funds, effectively encumbering the property and reducing its seizeable value — the creation of the mortgage is a transfer of property under this definition.

An accused in Kolkata enters into a partnership deed with a business associate, contributing his godown as a partnership asset, thereby changing legal ownership and control of the property to the firm — this constitutes a transfer of property.

A smuggler in Ahmedabad deliberately undervalues his share in a jointly owned plot and gifts it to his brother, intending to diminish his own property and increase his brother's — even this indirect value-shifting transaction qualifies as a transfer of property under the Act.

An accused person in Hyderabad grants a long-term lease of 30 years on his residential building to a shell company controlled by associates, locking the property beyond the reach of forfeiture proceedings — the grant of such a lease is included within the definition of transfer of property.
what_it_covers: Outright sale or conveyance of immovable or movable property to any third party by the accused.
Creation of a trust over the property, whether revocable or irrevocable, where the accused transfers property into a trust structure.
Grant or creation of a lease, mortgage, charge, easement, licence, or partnership interest over the property.
Exercise of a power of appointment by a person who is not the owner, directing the disposition of property to any person other than the donee of that power.
Any transaction intentionally designed to diminish the value of the accused's own property and correspondingly increase the value of another person's property, even if not a direct sale.
Assignment or settlement of property, including family settlements where property rights are redistributed among members to frustrate forfeiture.
what_it_excludes: Transactions that do not involve any change in ownership, control, or interest in the property — such as purely administrative internal re-classification of property records without any alienation.
Court-ordered transfers or dispositions made under a judicial order or decree that are not initiated by the accused for the purpose of frustrating forfeiture proceedings.
Routine payment of statutory dues such as property tax or municipal charges that do not transfer any ownership or interest in the property to another person.
Transfers confirmed or expressly permitted by the competent authority under section 68F itself, as these are expressly authorised and not prohibited dealings.
Seizure or freezing of property by an authorised officer, which is a State action and not a voluntary alienation by the owner.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition of 'transfer of property' determines the scope of the prohibition in section 68F: any such transfer made after a freezing order is issued, without prior permission of the officer or competent authority, is void and may be reversed in forfeiture proceedings. It directly governs whether an officer can seize or freeze property and whether a purported transfer by the accused can frustrate the State's right to forfeit illegally acquired property under Chapter VA of the NDPS Act.

transfer of property: A 'transfer of property' under this law means any way in which ownership, control, or benefit of a property is moved from one person to another. This includes selling, gifting, leasing, mortgaging, creating a trust, forming a partnership over the property, or any financial arrangement that shifts the property's value to someone else. Even transactions designed to reduce the value of a person's own property so that someone else benefits are treated as a transfer.

Legal text: For the purposes of section 68F, 'transfer of property' means any disposition, conveyance, assignment, settlement, delivery, payment or other alienation of property and, without limiting the generality of the foregoing, includes: the creation of a trust in property; the grant or creation of any lease, mortgage, charge, easement, licence, power, partnership or interest in property; the exercise of a power of appointment of property vested in any person, not the owner of the property, to determine its disposition in favour of any person other than the donee of the power; and any transaction entered into by any person with intent thereby to diminish directly or indirectly the value of his own property and to increase the value of the property of any other person.

Examples: A drug trafficker in Mumbai, facing investigation under NDPS Chapter VA, sells his flat in Andheri to a relative for a fraction of its market value to move it out of his name before forfeiture proceedings begin — this sale constitutes a 'transfer of property'. | An accused person in Delhi, whose properties are under inquiry, creates a trust naming his wife as trustee and transfers his farmland in Haryana into the trust to shield it from seizure — the creation of such a trust is explicitly covered as a transfer of property. | A narcotics offender in Chennai mortgages his commercial property to a private financier to raise funds, effectively encumbering the property and reducing its seizeable value — the creation of the mortgage is a transfer of property under this definition. | An accused in Kolkata enters into a partnership deed with a business associate, contributing his godown as a partnership asset, thereby changing legal ownership and control of the property to the firm — this constitutes a transfer of property. | A smuggler in Ahmedabad deliberately undervalues his share in a jointly owned plot and gifts it to his brother, intending to diminish his own property and increase his brother's — even this indirect value-shifting transaction qualifies as a transfer of property under the Act. | An accused person in Hyderabad grants a long-term lease of 30 years on his residential building to a shell company controlled by associates, locking the property beyond the reach of forfeiture proceedings — the grant of such a lease is included within the definition of transfer of property.

Tags: alienation of illegally acquired property, anti-forfeiture evasion, property disposition NDPS, freezing order trigger, trust creation as transfer, mortgage and encumbrance, value diminution transaction, Chapter VA forfeiture proceedings, concealment prevention mechanism, lease and licence as transfer, power of appointment property, drug proceeds asset transfer

Covers: Outright sale or conveyance of immovable or movable property to any third party by the accused.; Creation of a trust over the property, whether revocable or irrevocable, where the accused transfers property into a trust structure.; Grant or creation of a lease, mortgage, charge, easement, licence, or partnership interest over the property.; Exercise of a power of appointment by a person who is not the owner, directing the disposition of property to any person other than the donee of that power.; Any transaction intentionally designed to diminish the value of the accused's own property and correspondingly increase the value of another person's property, even if not a direct sale.; Assignment or settlement of property, including family settlements where property rights are redistributed among members to frustrate forfeiture.

Excludes: Transactions that do not involve any change in ownership, control, or interest in the property — such as purely administrative internal re-classification of property records without any alienation.; Court-ordered transfers or dispositions made under a judicial order or decree that are not initiated by the accused for the purpose of frustrating forfeiture proceedings.; Routine payment of statutory dues such as property tax or municipal charges that do not transfer any ownership or interest in the property to another person.; Transfers confirmed or expressly permitted by the competent authority under section 68F itself, as these are expressly authorised and not prohibited dealings.; Seizure or freezing of property by an authorised officer, which is a State action and not a voluntary alienation by the owner.

Why it matters: The definition of 'transfer of property' determines the scope of the prohibition in section 68F: any such transfer made after a freezing order is issued, without prior permission of the officer or competent authority, is void and may be reversed in forfeiture proceedings. It directly governs whether an officer can seize or freeze property and whether a purported transfer by the accused can frustrate the State's right to forfeit illegally acquired property under Chapter VA of the NDPS Act.

definitions.definition: A 'transferee in good faith' is a person who has acquired property for adequate consideration without knowledge or reasonable means of knowledge that the property was illegally acquired or traceable to illicit traffic in narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances, such that the acquisition is honest and without any intent to defeat the provisions of Chapter VA of the NDPS Act.
definitions.plain_english: A transferee in good faith is someone who bought or received property honestly, paying a fair price, without knowing (and without any reasonable way of knowing) that the property originally came from drug trafficking or other NDPS offences. Such a person is protected from having that property seized or forfeited under the law. In simple terms, it is an innocent buyer who had no idea about the illegal origins of what they purchased.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai flat-buyer purchases an apartment from a seller at full market rate through a registered sale deed, without any knowledge that the seller had previously been convicted under the NDPS Act for drug trafficking; the buyer is a transferee in good faith and the flat cannot be forfeited.

A Delhi businessman buys a commercial vehicle at auction from a used-car dealer at prevailing market price, unaware that the vehicle had earlier been held by a person involved in psychotropic substance smuggling; since he paid adequate consideration and had no knowledge of the tainted history, he qualifies as a transferee in good faith.

A Pune bank acquires a mortgaged agricultural plot through a court decree after the borrower defaults, without any knowledge that the land's original owner was an associate of an NDPS convict; the bank, having proceeded through legitimate legal process for adequate consideration, is protected as a transferee in good faith.

A Chennai jeweller purchases gold ornaments from a private individual at fair market value, the individual being a distant relative of an NDPS detenu, without any suspicion or notice of the connection to illicit drug proceeds; the jeweller would be regarded as a transferee in good faith, shielding the ornaments from forfeiture.

A Hyderabad real estate developer purchases land from a registered company at market rate, not knowing that a director of that company had an outstanding arrest warrant under the NDPS Act; provided the developer conducted normal due diligence and paid full consideration, they may be treated as a transferee in good faith.
what_it_covers: A buyer who purchases property at fair market value through a registered transaction without any notice of the seller's NDPS conviction or the property's illicit origins.
A financial institution (such as a bank) that acquires property through a lawful mortgage enforcement or court decree for adequate consideration without knowledge of NDPS taint.
A subsequent holder in a chain of title where an intermediate transferee paid full consideration and had no actual or constructive knowledge of the illegally acquired nature of the property.

A relative or associate of an NDPS-covered person who independently acquired specific property for adequate consideration before any NDPS proceedings were initiated and without knowledge of the illicit connection.
what_it_excludes: A person who acquires property at a grossly undervalued price (not constituting adequate consideration), which raises presumption of knowledge of its tainted origin.
A close associate or family member who receives property as a gift or without any real consideration from a person covered under Section 68A, as there is no payment of adequate consideration.
A person who had actual knowledge or reasonable notice (e.g., through public NDPS proceedings or official notifications) that the property was illegally acquired at the time of acquisition.
A person who acquires property through a sham transaction or as a benami arrangement designed to shield it from forfeiture, where the transfer is not a genuine arms-length transaction.
Any holder who acquired property after the initiation of freezing or forfeiture proceedings under Chapter VA, where public notice of the taint was available.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as a 'transferee in good faith for adequate consideration' is decisive in determining whether property held by them can be forfeited under Chapter VA of the NDPS Act — if this definition applies, the property is excluded from the definition of 'illegally acquired property' and is shielded from forfeiture proceedings initiated by the competent authority; if it does not apply, the property remains liable to forfeiture even in the hands of a subsequent innocent-seeming holder.

definitions.definition: Transhipment, as used in the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, refers to the act of transferring narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances from one conveyance to another, or through Indian territory, in the course of their movement from one country or place to another, without the goods entering the stream of domestic trade. It is listed as a constituent activity of 'illicit traffic' under Section 2(viiia) when conducted outside the permissions granted under the Act.
definitions.plain_english: Transhipment means moving drugs or psychotropic substances from one ship, aircraft, or vehicle to another while passing through India on their way to a final destination in another country. It is essentially a transit operation where the drugs do not enter Indian trade but pass through Indian ports, airports, or territory. When done without proper authorization, it is treated as a serious criminal offence under the NDPS Act.
real_world_examples: A consignment of heroin packed in commercial cargo arrives at Chennai Port from Afghanistan, is offloaded from one container vessel, and transferred onto another ship bound for Australia — this transit transfer through Indian territorial waters constitutes transhipment under the NDPS Act.

At Indira Gandhi International Airport, New Delhi, a passenger's checked-in luggage containing methamphetamine is transferred from a flight arriving from Myanmar to a connecting flight departing to the United Kingdom without clearing Indian customs — this act of transfer qualifies as transhipment.

A fishing trawler intercepted in Indian Exclusive Economic Zone waters is found to be transferring packets of hashish from a larger vessel to a smaller speedboat for onward delivery to a Southeast Asian port, constituting illegal transhipment under Section 23 of the NDPS Act.

Narcotic Control Bureau officers at Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust in Mumbai intercept a container in which cocaine consigned from South America to Europe is being shifted from one shipping line's container to another — this mid-route transfer through Indian port infrastructure is treated as transhipment.

A drug trafficking syndicate uses a free trade zone at an Indian port to repack and transfer cannabis resin from a vessel arriving from Pakistan to a cargo ship bound for Malaysia, exploiting the transit facility — this operation is prosecuted as illegal transhipment under the NDPS Act.
what_it_covers: Transfer of narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances from one ship to another within Indian territorial waters or ports while the consignment is in transit to a foreign destination.
Movement of narcotic drugs through Indian airports involving transfer between international flights without the substance entering domestic Indian trade or consumption.
Transfer of psychotropic substances from one mode of conveyance (e.g., truck) to another (e.g., vessel) within Indian land borders for onward movement to a third country.
Reloading or reshipping of narcotic drugs at Indian free trade zones, special economic zones, or bonded warehouses as part of an international trafficking route.
Any intermediate offloading and re-loading of controlled substances on Indian soil, in Indian ports, or in Indian airspace as part of a through-transit operation.
what_it_excludes: Import into India, which involves narcotic drugs entering Indian territory for domestic use, trade, or consumption — this is a separate, distinct activity under the Act.
Export from India, which covers dispatch of narcotic drugs originating from Indian territory to a foreign country — distinguished from transhipment where the drugs merely pass through.
Domestic transport or inter-state movement of narcotic drugs within India between two Indian locations, which is governed separately under the transport provisions of the Act.
Lawful transhipment operations conducted under a valid licence, permit, or authorisation issued by competent authorities under the NDPS Act and applicable rules.
Seizure or controlled delivery operations authorised under Section 50A, where suspect consignments are allowed to pass through India under official supervision as an investigative technique.
definitions.why_it_matters: Transhipment without lawful authorisation constitutes a punishable offence under Section 23 of the NDPS Act, attracting rigorous imprisonment of up to ten years and fine for small quantities, and up to twenty years rigorous imprisonment and fine for commercial quantities. It also forms a component of 'illicit traffic' under Section 2(viiia), making a person liable for preventive detention under the PITNDPS Act and triggering asset forfeiture provisions under Chapter VA of the Act.

definitions.definition: "Transport" is not formally defined in Section 2 of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985; however, as used in Sections 17 and 18, it means the physical carrying, conveying, or moving of narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances from one place to another, whether within a state or across state boundaries, by any means or mode whatsoever, including by land, water, or air, using any conveyance or by a person on their own body.
definitions.plain_english: Transport means physically moving or carrying illegal drugs or controlled substances from one location to another. This includes moving them by truck, car, train, boat, aircraft, or even on foot or concealed on a person's body. It does not matter whether the movement is over a short or long distance — any deliberate physical movement of prohibited substances counts as transport under this law.
real_world_examples: A truck driver in Rajasthan is intercepted by NCB officers while carrying 10 kg of opium hidden inside a false compartment of his goods vehicle travelling from Chittorgarh to Delhi — this constitutes transport of opium under Section 17.

A man is arrested at Chennai Central Railway Station with 500 grams of heroin strapped to his body in a specially stitched inner garment while boarding a train to Bengaluru — the act of boarding the train with the drugs amounts to transport of a manufactured drug under Section 17.

A fishing trawler operating off the coast of Gujarat is intercepted by the Indian Coast Guard carrying 200 kg of cannabis concealed beneath the fish cargo — moving the cannabis across coastal waters constitutes transport under Section 18.

A courier employee in Punjab knowingly delivers parcels containing psychotropic tablets packed as medicines from Amritsar to Ludhiana on behalf of a drug syndicate — the act of conveying the parcels from one city to another amounts to transport under the NDPS Act.

A mule hired by a drug cartel carries packets of brown sugar (heroin) on his person across a state border from Bihar into West Bengal by boarding a passenger bus — this constitutes transport regardless of the quantity carried.

An autorickshaw driver in Mumbai is used by traffickers to move small consignments of charas between two neighbourhoods repeatedly — each such movement constitutes transport of cannabis under Section 18.
semantic_tags: narcotic drug movement by land water air
what_it_covers: Carrying narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances in a vehicle (car, truck, auto, bus, train) from one location to another, regardless of state boundaries.
Moving prohibited substances concealed on a person's body, in clothing, luggage, or personal effects while travelling.
Transporting drugs via waterways or coastal routes using boats, trawlers, or vessels.
Movement of narcotics by air, including concealment in checked baggage or cargo on domestic or international flights.
Any organised movement of drugs by a courier, delivery agent, or hired mule acting on behalf of a drug syndicate.
Short-distance local transport of prohibited substances, such as within a city or between adjacent localities.
what_it_excludes: Stationary possession of narcotics at a fixed location, such as storing drugs in a warehouse or residence, which falls under possession rather than transport.
The mere manufacture or production of narcotic drugs at a site, where no movement from that site to another location has yet occurred.
Import into India from a foreign country or export from India to a foreign country, which are separately defined and governed by distinct provisions of the Act.
Transhipment of drugs through Indian territory under a formally authorised and supervised controlled delivery operation under Section 50A.
Movement of narcotics by a licensed authority (such as a government factory or licensed dealer) in strict compliance with permits and authorisations issued under the Act.
Personal consumption of a small quantity at the same location where it was obtained, where no movement to another place is involved.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as 'transport' under the NDPS Act is critical because Sections 17 and 18 prescribe severe penalties — ranging from rigorous imprisonment of up to 10 years for small quantities to 10 to 20 years (extendable to death in repeat offences) for commercial quantities of manufactured drugs and cannabis respectively — triggered specifically by the act of transportation. Establishing transport as the offence also determines jurisdiction, the applicable presumption of culpable mental state under Section 35, and eligibility for bail restrictions under Section 37.

definitions.definition: 'trust' includes any other legal obligation.
definitions.plain_english: Under the NDPS Act, a 'trust' is not limited to a formal trust deed registered under law. It covers any legal arrangement or obligation where one person holds or manages property on behalf of another. This broad definition ensures that drug traffickers cannot hide their illegally acquired assets by routing them through trusts or similar legal structures.
real_world_examples: A drug trafficker in Mumbai creates a registered family trust in his wife's name and transfers proceeds from narcotics sales into it to disguise ownership; the competent authority treats the trust as falling within this definition and proceeds with forfeiture under Chapter VA.

A kingpin in Punjab sets up a charitable trust ostensibly for social welfare but actually uses it to park illegally acquired property worth crores; the NDPS competent authority identifies the trust assets as liable to forfeiture since the trafficker contributed more than 20% of the trust's value.

A Delhi-based narcotics dealer informally instructs his accountant to hold agricultural land 'on trust' for him without any written deed; under the NDPS definition, this informal legal obligation qualifies as a 'trust', making the accountant an 'associate' and the land subject to freezing and forfeiture.

A narcotics financier in Kolkata routes drug money through a Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) arrangement, which functions as a legal obligation among co-parceners; the competent authority treats this HUF obligation as a 'trust' under Section 68B and proceeds to identify and freeze the property under Section 68F.

A drug lord in Rajasthan transfers hawala proceeds into a Waqf-like endowment structure managed by a trusted associate; the broad NDPS definition of 'trust' encompasses this religious endowment obligation, enabling authorities to trace and forfeit the illegally acquired property held within it.
what_it_covers: A formally registered trust deed under the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, created by a person whose property is liable to forfeiture under Chapter VA of the NDPS Act.
Any informal or oral legal obligation where a person holds property on behalf of a drug trafficker, even without a written trust instrument.
Religious, charitable, or family endowment structures (such as HUF arrangements or Waqf-like entities) that function as legal obligations and are used to hold illegally acquired property.
A trust where the drug offender has contributed assets amounting to 20% or more of the trust's total value, making the trustee an 'associate' under Section 68B.
Any other legal obligation that mirrors the function of a trust in holding, managing, or concealing property derived from narcotics contraventions.
what_it_excludes: A bona fide trust created by a person with no connection to narcotics offences, where the trust assets are entirely legitimate and unrelated to any contravention of the NDPS Act.

A transferee in good faith for adequate consideration who received trust property without knowledge of its illegal origin, as protected under the definition of 'illegally acquired property' in Section 68B.

Purely contractual arrangements that do not create any fiduciary or legal obligation to hold property on behalf of another, such as a standard sale agreement or loan transaction with no trust element.
Statutory public trusts or government-administered bodies that are fully regulated and audited by public authorities and bear no nexus to any narcotics-related contravention.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an arrangement qualifies as a 'trust' under Section 68B determines whether the trustee is classified as an 'associate' of the drug offender, making both the trustee and the trust's assets liable to inquiry, freezing under Section 68F, and ultimate forfeiture under Chapter VA of the NDPS Act. A broad interpretation prevents drug traffickers from shielding illegally acquired property behind formal or informal trust structures.

definitions.definition: A trustee, in the context of Chapter VA of the NDPS Act, refers to the trustee of any trust where the trust has been created by a person whose property is liable to be forfeited, or where the value of assets contributed by such person to the trust amounts to not less than twenty per cent of the value of the assets of the trust on the date of contribution; such trustee is classified as an 'associate' of that person and is subject to notice and proceedings under section 68L regarding illegally acquired property held in trust.
definitions.plain_english: A trustee is the person who legally holds and manages assets or property placed in a trust. Under the NDPS Act, if the person who created the trust or contributed significantly to it is suspected of acquiring property through drug trafficking, the trustee managing that trust can be called upon to explain where the money or assets came from. This means the trustee can be drawn into forfeiture proceedings even if they personally had no involvement in any drug-related offence.
real_world_examples: A drug trafficker in Mumbai creates a family trust and transfers three residential flats into it, appointing his brother as trustee. The Competent Authority under the NDPS Act serves a notice on the brother-trustee under Section 68L asking him to explain the source of funds used to acquire those flats.

A narcotics dealer in Delhi contributes ₹2 crore out of a total trust corpus of ₹5 crore (i.e., 40%) to a charitable trust registered in his wife's name, appointing a family advocate as trustee. The trustee receives a notice from the Competent Authority to explain the origin of the contributed assets.

A person convicted under the NDPS Act had earlier set up a business trust in Hyderabad, transferring factory machinery and land to it, with a friend appointed as trustee. During forfeiture proceedings, the trustee is treated as an associate and is required to account for how the trust property was acquired.

In a Kolkata-based case, a psychotropic substance smuggler contributes gold ornaments worth ₹80 lakh to an existing family trust valued at ₹3 crore, making him a contributor of over 20%. The appointed trustee is served notice under Section 68L and all Chapter VA provisions apply to the trust property.

A narcotics kingpin in Chennai creates a private trust for the benefit of his minor children and appoints a chartered accountant as trustee. After the kingpin's arrest, the Competent Authority identifies real estate held by the trust as illegally acquired property and serves notice on the trustee to explain the source of funds used to purchase it.
what_it_covers: A person appointed as trustee of a trust that was created by someone whose property is liable to be forfeited under Chapter VA of the NDPS Act.
A trustee of a trust to which a person suspected of drug-related offences has contributed assets amounting to at least twenty per cent of the total trust value on the date of contribution.

A trustee who holds property on behalf of a trust where the Competent Authority has reason to believe the property is illegally acquired, and who is subject to a notice under Section 68L to explain the source of such assets.
A trustee of any legal obligation (since 'trust' includes any other legal obligation under Section 68B) where such obligation was created or substantially funded by a person covered under Chapter VA.
what_it_excludes: A trustee of a trust to which the suspect contributed less than twenty per cent of the trust's total asset value, unless the trust was originally created by that suspect.
A transferee in good faith for adequate consideration who subsequently manages trust assets without knowledge of the illegal origin of the funds.

A trustee of a government-recognised public charitable trust with no nexus to any person whose property is liable to be forfeited under Chapter VA, even if the trust incidentally received a donation from such a person below the twenty per cent threshold.
A nominee director or officer of a corporate body who manages corporate assets, as opposed to a trustee managing trust property specifically covered by sub-clause (vi) of clause (b) of Section 68B.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of a person as a trustee under Chapter VA of the NDPS Act makes them an 'associate' of the person whose property is subject to forfeiture, thereby triggering their obligation to respond to notices under Section 68L and exposing the trust property to freezing, seizure, and forfeiture proceedings. Failure to satisfactorily explain the source of trust assets can result in the forfeiture of those assets to the Central Government under the Act.

definitions.definition: The term 'use' is not independently defined in Section 2 of the NDPS Act, 1985, but appears within the definition of 'illicit traffic' as one of the prohibited activities in relation to narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances. In context, 'use' refers to the act of employing or applying a narcotic drug or psychotropic substance for personal consumption or any other purpose, without lawful authorisation under the Act or the rules, orders, or licences issued thereunder.
definitions.plain_english: In the NDPS Act, 'use' means physically employing or consuming a narcotic drug or psychotropic substance. This includes taking a drug into one's body or applying it for any purpose without permission from the government. If someone uses such a substance without a valid licence or authorisation, it can be treated as part of illegal drug trafficking under the law.
real_world_examples: A person in Mumbai is found injecting heroin for recreational purposes without any medical prescription or government authorisation — this constitutes 'use' of a narcotic drug and falls within illicit traffic under the NDPS Act.
A resident of Delhi is caught smoking cannabis (ganja) for personal enjoyment without a valid permit, making the act an instance of 'use' of a narcotic drug as prohibited under the Act.

A patient in Chennai who consumes morphine tablets obtained without a valid medical prescription and beyond the scope of any authorised medical treatment is engaged in unauthorised 'use' of a manufactured narcotic drug.

A college student in Pune who snorts cocaine obtained from an illicit source for recreational purposes is found to be engaged in the 'use' of a coca derivative, which amounts to illicit traffic under Section 2 of the NDPS Act.
A labourer in Assam who consumes opium regularly without holding any government-issued permit or licence is engaging in the 'use' of opium, rendering such activity an offence under the NDPS Act.
what_it_covers: Consuming a narcotic drug such as heroin, cocaine, or opium for personal recreational or habitual use without valid authorisation.
Ingesting, injecting, inhaling, or otherwise applying a psychotropic substance for any purpose not sanctioned by a licence, permit, or authorisation under the NDPS Act.
Employing a controlled narcotic drug for self-medication or any non-medical purpose without a valid prescription or government approval.
Repeated or habitual consumption of cannabis products like ganja or charas outside the scope of any lawful exemption or permit.
what_it_excludes: Medical consumption of essential narcotic drugs by a patient under a valid prescription issued by a licensed medical practitioner within the framework permitted by the Act.
Scientific or research-based use of narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances by authorised institutions holding valid licences or permits granted by the Central Government.
Use of narcotic or psychotropic substances by government-authorised personnel in the course of official duties such as forensic analysis, testing, or destruction of seized drugs.
Consumption of substances that do not fall within the statutory definitions of narcotic drugs, psychotropic substances, or controlled substances under the NDPS Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as 'use' under the NDPS Act determines whether it falls within the definition of 'illicit traffic', thereby attracting penal consequences including prosecution, preventive detention under the PITNDPS Act, and forfeiture of illegally acquired property. Establishing 'use' is also relevant to identifying a person as an 'addict' under Section 2, which affects their eligibility for treatment and immunity provisions under the Act.

definitions.definition: A warrant of arrest, as used in the NDPS Act under Section 68Z, refers to a formal judicial or authorised order issued against a person directing their arrest in connection with offences under this Act or any corresponding law of another country, and which, when withdrawn, triggers the mandatory release of property seized or frozen under Chapter VA of the Act.
definitions.plain_english: A warrant of arrest is an official legal document that orders law enforcement to arrest a specific person suspected of a drug-related offence. Under the NDPS Act, when such a warrant is withdrawn against a person, any property that was seized or frozen because of that person's suspected involvement must be released. It is essentially the trigger that links a person's arrest proceedings to the fate of their frozen or seized assets.
real_world_examples: A court in Mumbai issues a warrant of arrest against a person accused of financing narcotics trafficking; the NCB freezes his bank accounts and property under Chapter VA. If the warrant is later withdrawn, all frozen property must be released under Section 68Z.

An Indian national faces charges under a corresponding law in Singapore for drug trafficking; Indian authorities issue a warrant of arrest and seize his Delhi property. Upon withdrawal of the warrant, the seized property in India stands released.

A Kolkata-based associate of a drug cartel has a warrant of arrest issued against him under the NDPS Act. After investigation reveals mistaken identity and the warrant is formally withdrawn, his frozen residential property is released by the competent authority.

A Punjab landowner is named in a warrant of arrest for alleged opium cultivation on his land; his agricultural property is frozen under Chapter VA. When the warrant is subsequently withdrawn due to lack of evidence, the property is mandatorily released under Section 68Z.

An accused drug financier's warrant of arrest is issued and his business assets are seized. Upon the prosecution withdrawing the warrant following a negotiated settlement or exoneration, all seized business assets must stand released under the provisions of Section 68Z.
what_it_covers: A formal court-issued order directing the arrest of a person accused of offences under the NDPS Act.
An arrest warrant issued in connection with a corresponding law of another country that has bearing on property seized in India under Chapter VA.
An authorised order of arrest (whether judicial or issued by a competent authority) that, when withdrawn, mandates the release of seized or frozen property under Section 68Z.
Warrants issued against persons falling under clause (a), (b), or (cc) of sub-section (2) of Section 68A of the NDPS Act.
what_it_excludes: A detention order issued under preventive detention laws, which is separately addressed in Section 68Z and is distinct from a warrant of arrest.
An authorisation of arrest, which is a separate term under the NDPS Act and operates independently of a warrant of arrest.
Summons or notices to appear before a court or authority, which do not constitute a warrant of arrest and do not trigger the same property-release consequences under Section 68Z.
Search or seizure warrants, which authorise investigation actions but are not directed at arresting a person and do not fall within the meaning of a warrant of arrest under Section 68Z.
definitions.why_it_matters: The existence or withdrawal of a warrant of arrest directly determines whether property seized or frozen under Chapter VA of the NDPS Act must be released; withdrawal of the warrant against an accused person is one of the statutory conditions that compels the competent authority to release such property under Section 68Z. This makes the warrant of arrest a critical procedural document that links criminal proceedings against an individual to the civil consequences of asset forfeiture under the Act.
